MONDAY 5 OCT 2026

UNITED STATES — S&P GLOBAL SERVICES PMI FINAL / COMPOSITE PMI FINAL (Sep)

Release Date: 5 Oct 2026 | Local Time: 15:45 (Paris)
Importance: ***

PM FLASH: Services PMI rose to 58.8 (58.7 flash; 56.5 August); composite reached 58.4. Stronger domestic orders, hiring and backlogs coincided with faster input and selling-price inflation.

PM READ-THROUGH: Services-led growth accelerated with broader industry participation, but the loss of August’s favorable pricing offset deepens the inflation constraint without confirming economy-wide hiring strength.

PM DEBATE & KEY TAKEAWAYS: Professional insight: The supplier survey maps activity to about 4% annualized Q3 GDP, substantially firmer than expenditure-based tracking; these are different estimation methods. The key surprise is simultaneous demand breadth and cost acceleration. Check realized services spending and hiring, not diffusion alone.

1. Reuters Data

S&P Global Comp PMI Final: 58,4 | Prior: 58,4

S&P Global Svcs PMI Final: 58,8 | Prior: 58,7

2. Professional Market Commentary

The final September report portrayed the strongest services expansion since July 2021, composite output at a five-year high, accelerating domestic new business, hiring at its strongest since June 2022, and exceptionally rapid backlog growth. All five major services sectors expanded for the first time in ten months, with transport/storage returning to growth and information/communication still leading. Input costs increased at the strongest diffusion since November 2022 and selling prices at the second-fastest rate in just over a year; energy, freight and some labor costs featured prominently.

Chris Williamson (S&P Global) highlighted strength extending beyond technology into consumer-facing, financial, health and industrial services. His survey-based mapping suggested around 4% annualized Q3 GDP growth and an even faster September output pace; this is a diffusion-to-GDP model, not national-accounts evidence. TheStreet Pro highlighted strong orders/hiring/backlogs alongside operating-cost reacceleration and cross-sector breadth. No separately attributable named bank economist focusing on this final S&P release or independent Tier-1 debate was established. No independent market move can be allocated to S&P: ISM followed 15 minutes later.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment

The survey supports a convincing continuation of the July–September services upturn, reinforced by wider domestic orders, hiring and backlogs. The new macro increment is a more inflation-constrained growth mix. Survey diffusion is not a measure of output growth or payroll additions; the sharply stronger S&P survey differs materially from ISM and weak realized payrolls.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms

Activity and demand. Services PMI progressed 54.6 in July, 56.5 in August and 58.8 in September; composite output 56.0 → 58.4 from August. New services business expanded at the fastest pace in roughly four-and-a-half years, led by US customers; export orders rose more modestly for a second month. Higher output across all five sectors is stronger evidence than a technology-only rebound. Survey levels do not translate directly into a particular GDP growth rate or actual job creation.

Backlogs and capacity. Backlogs increased for a nineteenth successive month at a near-historical pace, supporting ongoing activity but also potentially reflecting transport/logistics bottlenecks and delayed fulfillment rather than an unambiguous rise in final demand. More orders plus incomplete execution increase near-term business visibility without proving unconstrained capacity.

Labor divergence. Services hiring diffusion reached its strongest since June 2022 and expanded for a third month, yet ISM Services Employment was only 50.1 and the contemporaneously cited September payroll change only 29k, with unemployment 4.2%. S&P and ISM have different panels and constructions; diffusion measures the distribution of hiring, not its absolute level. The evidence indicates broader willingness to hire, not verified national payroll reacceleration.

Inflation and expectations. Input inflation reached its fastest since November 2022; output-price increases were near a one-year high, reversing August moderation. Gasoline, fuel, freight and some labor costs feature prominently. This is consistent with later CPI/PPI cost deterioration but cannot be translated one-for-one into consumer-price inflation. Business expectations improved to a one-year high on product launches, customer acquisition and anticipated recovery even as fuel costs rose; the survey closed 28 September, before later price releases.

ISM reconciliation and GDP mapping. S&P accelerates strongly while ISM Business Activity falls 61.7 → 56.5, although both show high orders/backlogs and firmer prices. S&P's activity index differs from the four-component ISM composite (including inverse supplier deliveries), but the underlying activity and employment disagreement remains genuine. Williamson’s roughly 4% Q3 GDP mapping contrasts with approximately 3% expenditure-based tracking; methods differ, so hard GDP/PCE evidence should determine the realized path.

C. State Transition & Historical Context

State transition: continuation of activity acceleration with inflation deterioration — stronger orders, hiring and sector breadth extend the services expansion while reversing August’s price moderation; growth resilience becomes increasingly inflation-constrained.

Context from prior regional live file: July S&P Services established a recovery from the weak spring; August extended it to 56.5, partly via deferred spending, while price pressure moderated. September reaches 58.8 with stronger demand and hiring but a more adverse input/output pricing profile.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: The release upgrades services growth confidence but removes August’s benign pricing offset. Strong business conditions provide growth cover for Fed restriction, while the price data increase inflation-persistence risk; labor reacceleration is not proven.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: If higher backlogs represent genuine order growth and broad hiring becomes realized payroll gains, continued tight policy gains justification. If rising input costs and bottlenecks mainly produce price increases without real-volume growth, survey strength can be backward-looking and a supply shock can impair demand. No independent S&P-specific market repricing was established.

What to verify next: October S&P flash and ISM services orders/prices/employment; real services PCE, personal income and payrolls; fulfillment/backlogs after transport disruptions.

Macro configuration: strong services demand + broadened sector output + backlog/capacity friction + improved hiring diffusion + renewed selling-price inflation.

UNITED STATES — ISM SERVICES PMI (Sep)

Release Date: 5 Oct 2026 | Local Time: 16:00 (Paris)
Importance: ***

PM FLASH: ISM Services slipped to 54.9 from 55.4 (55.2 poll); Business Activity fell 5.2 points, but orders held at 59.8 and Prices Paid hit 74.0.

PM READ-THROUGH: An unremarkable headline miss masks activity moderation and persistent demand, while the highest input-cost diffusion since July 2022 is the clear policy-relevant deterioration.

PM DEBATE & KEY TAKEAWAYS: Professional insight: The apparent activity slowdown and strong orders can coexist via slower fulfillment and inventory accumulation. Employment only barely returned to expansion, contrasting with S&P hiring. The next test is whether price diffusion survives falling fuel costs or spreads to realized core services.

1. Reuters Data

ISM N-Mfg PMI: 54,9 | Prior: 55,4 | Poll: 55,2 | Surprise: -0,30

2. Professional Market Commentary

Institutional commentary interpreted 54.9 as moderation from August’s exceptionally high services activity, not a demand break. Business Activity eased substantially; New Orders remained high, Employment returned just above neutral, and Prices Paid advanced to 74.0. Fuel, tariffs and supply shortages figured prominently in comments.

Kurt Rankin (PNC Economics) treated the small headline miss as benign given order books, better survey employment and credit support; PNC envisaged two additional 25bp hikes through early 2027. Admir Kolaj (TD Economics) stressed broad cost pressure and slower deliveries and expected another Fed hike before year-end. ISM’s Steve Miller highlighted fuel as the most widely cited constraint and linked marginal hiring improvement to backlogs. House disagreement concerned activity normalization versus nascent deceleration, not whether services cost pressure was intensifying. No reliable market move attributable solely to ISM was found, including because S&P released 15 minutes earlier.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment

ISM activity loses momentum from August’s exceptional peak, but New Orders 59.8 and growing backlogs prevent a contraction narrative. The distinctive issue is the cost shock: Prices Paid at 74.0 reflects unusually widespread input inflation while hiring remains marginally positive and some rate-sensitive sectors are weakening.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms

Composition (Aug → Sep): Headline 55.4 → 54.9 (-0.5); Business Activity 61.7 → 56.5 (-5.2); New Orders 60.9 → 59.8 (-1.1); Employment 47.8 → 50.1 (+2.3); Supplier Deliveries 51.3 → 53.2 (+1.9); Prices Paid 72.6 → 74.0 (+1.4); Backlogs 55.6 → 56.6 (+1.0); Inventories 56.7 → 57.8 (+1.1); New Export Orders 56.3 → 46.9 (-9.4). The headline understates activity moderation because its equal-weight components include slower supplier deliveries, which mechanically lifts ISM even when attributable to bottlenecks.

Demand, backlogs, inventories. Orders near 60 despite current activity cooling can support future production; backlog expansion and inventories also reflect delivery delays, precautionary purchases and possible anticipated cost increases. Exact backlog source conflict: ISM’s summary and detail tables say 56.6; one explanatory sentence says 58.3. Retain 56.6 but do not assert an exact backlog historical rank. New export orders contracted to 46.9; approximately 39% of respondents do not measure exports, reducing inference confidence. PNC’s euro-competitiveness interpretation is a house hypothesis, not independently established cause.

Employment and interest sensitivity. Employment at 50.1 is barely above neutral: 16.5% reported more staff, 16.2% fewer and 67.3% unchanged; March–September average around 48.2. This is consistent with low-hire/low-fire rather than strong payroll growth. Construction uniquely reported lower new orders for a second month, with financing qualification, housing and bank-funding concerns prominent.

Inflation and supply chains. Prices Paid reached its highest level since July 2022 and exceeded 70 in six of seven months. Seventeen industries reported rising prices; none reported declines. Fuel advanced for an eighth month, with diesel, gasoline, software licenses, memory, metals and electric equipment. Supplier Deliveries increased to 53.2; shortages included computers, fuel, memory, SSDs, steel, switchgear, wire/cable. Energy/logistics and AI/data-center components may have different persistence. Prices Paid measures breadth, not the percentage change, and input costs are not a direct CPI forecast.

Cross-release reconciliation. S&P signaled acceleration and much stronger hiring; ISM sees activity slowing and hiring near flat. Both confirm resilient new business/backlogs and higher cost diffusion, subsequently corroborated directionally by realized PPI and CPI, though pass-through into final consumer services remains unquantified.

C. State Transition & Historical Context

State transition: stabilization in activity / deterioration in inflation — services remain firmly expansionary after August’s surge, marginal survey hiring stabilizes, and exceptionally widespread input costs become a stronger constraint.

Context from prior regional live file: July ISM showed strong demand with weak employment and rising prices; August activity and orders accelerated to 61.7 and 60.9 while employment stayed contractionary. September moderates output, retains strong orders, nudges employment above 50 and lifts Prices Paid to 74.0.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: ISM adds an independent, price-intensive warning to S&P’s strong services signal. The central issue is sustained orders with broad cost inflation rather than the modest headline miss.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: Input prices and logistics pressure can reflect energy-related supply inflation rather than pure domestic overheating; employment and construction weakness constrain an immediate-hike inference. PNC and TD maintained later tightening expectations but did not establish an October requirement. If new orders stay near 60 and core-PCE pricing confirms persistence, further Fed action gains support; falling orders and hiring would strengthen the demand-damage interpretation.

What to verify next: October ISM prices/business activity/new orders, S&P reconciliation, core-PCE services, payrolls, construction/housing and energy-price persistence.

Macro configuration: resilient services demand + slower current output + marginal hiring improvement + price diffusion at multi-year high + pockets of rate sensitivity.

WEDNESDAY 14 OCT 2026

UNITED STATES — CPI / CORE CPI / CPI-W (Sep)

Release Date: 14 Oct 2026 | Local Time: 14:30 (Paris)
Importance: ****

PM FLASH: Core CPI increased 0.3% m/m versus 0.2% expected for a second consecutive month; headline rose 0.6%, as gasoline +9.1% drove over half the advance.

PM READ-THROUGH: Energy explains the headline surge, but firmer core goods and non-energy services lift persistence risk while falling real wages raise the prospect of future consumption damage.

PM DEBATE & KEY TAKEAWAYS: Debate: Additional Fed tightening attracted broad agreement, but an October hike remained contested versus a December move. Key takeaways: Underlying rents stayed relatively contained; transport, recreation and education suggest selective core breadth. Separate energy pass-through from sustained domestic pricing using core-PCE services.

1. Reuters Data

Core CPI MM, SA: 0,3% | Prior: 0,3% | Poll: 0,2% | Surprise: 0,10%

Core CPI YY, NSA: 2,6% | Prior: 2,4% | Poll: 2,5% | Surprise: 0,10%

CPI MM, SA: 0,6% | Prior: 0,4% | Poll: 0,6% | Surprise: 0,00%

CPI YY, NSA: 3,7% | Prior: 3,4% | Poll: 3,6% | Surprise: 0,10%

CPI Wage Earner: 330,654 | Prior: 328,481

2. Professional Market Commentary

The professional tape described an energy-led headline shock with a less benign underlying broadening: September headline CPI matched the +0.6% monthly poll, but core +0.3% exceeded +0.2% expected for a second month. Core inflation was firmer across selected services and goods; sharply higher gasoline, transportation and airfares tightened the household real-income constraint.

Timing disagreement: James McCann (Edward Jones), Chris Zaccarelli (Northlight), Shawn Snyder (Potomac) and First Trust supported additional late-2026 restriction, usually October hold / December hike, rather than a mechanically immediate move. Stephanie Roth (Wolfe Research), Stephen Brown (Capital Economics) and Anshul Sharma (Savvy Wealth) argued the broader core print reopened the October question. George Brown (Schroders) stressed domestic persistence and the need for sustained restriction. Adam Schickling (Vanguard) expected productivity, slower wages and consumer price sensitivity eventually to restrain prices. First Trust emphasized the Fed cannot reverse an external energy-supply disruption with rates alone; Peter Andersen (Andersen Capital Management) questioned extra tightening amid deteriorating consumer purchasing power.

Verified contemporaneous post-CPI snapshots: UST 2Y +13bp to 4.92%; UST 10Y +9bp to 5.304%; curve approximately 4bp flatter; DXY +0.55% to 102.75; S&P 500 -0.4% at open, Nasdaq -0.6%, gold -1.6% to $4,088/oz. These are snapshots, not closing returns. The internally consistent CME FedWatch comparison relayed by Fox Business increased October hike odds 22.1% → 41.5%; other Reuters probability claims conflicted and remain flagged.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment

September shows an adverse shift beyond a one-month energy disturbance. Core +0.3% m/m for the second month and 3m annualized around 3.4% indicate persistence in selected goods and services, whereas the largest headline contribution originates in petroleum products. Real wage declines establish a potential subsequent demand restraint that should not be confused with immediate disinflation.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms

Energy and headline. Headline CPI +0.6% m/m (+3.7% y/y versus 3.4%), with energy +5.2% m/m / +20.4% y/y and gasoline +9.1% / +34.2% explaining more than half the monthly rise. Fuel oil +15.3% m/m / +74.2% y/y; energy services only +0.1% m/m. Aggregate food unchanged; groceries -0.1%, food away from home +0.2%. This is concentrated petroleum inflation, not a contemporaneous across-the-board household energy/food acceleration.

Core momentum: Core +0.3% m/m and 2.6% y/y (2.4% prior), 3m annualized 3.4%, 6m 2.9%. First Trust's derived annualized sequential measures: headline 4.6% (3m) / 3.7% (6m); excluding energy 3.1% / 2.8%; services excluding energy 3.8% / 3.6%. August’s roughly 2% 3m core pace rose to 3.4%. These are annualizations from underlying indexes, not direct year-on-year comparisons.

Services composition. Services excluding energy services +0.4% m/m versus +0.3%; shelter +0.4% versus +0.3%, but OER +0.3% (0.2% previous), primary residence rents +0.2% unchanged, lodging away from home +2.0% after +2.4%. Non-rent services: transportation +0.6% after +0.5%; airfares +1.2% after +2.7% and +22.4% y/y; recreation +0.5% after unchanged; education +0.6%; medical care services +0.3% after -0.2%. Fuel plausibly affects airfares but cannot explain all domestic categories. A clean ex-shelter/ex-energy supercore reading requires explicit measurement, not inference from services excluding energy alone.

Core goods composition. Core goods +0.3% m/m after +0.1%, including used vehicles +0.7% (third consecutive rise), new vehicles +0.2%, apparel +0.3%, tobacco +0.7%. Offsets: medical commodities -0.7%, household furnishings/supplies -0.2%, communication -0.2%. Core goods still only +0.7% y/y, limiting a generalized goods-inflation-breakout narrative.

Real-income counter-signal. First Trust estimated real average hourly earnings -0.5% m/m and -0.7% y/y, real weekly earnings -0.1% y/y. Fuel and non-energy inflation impair discretionary purchasing power. Inflation can intensify before household demand weakens, making an automatic demand-overheating diagnosis hazardous.

C. State Transition & Historical Context

State transition: deterioration — a second +0.3% core reading, firmer core goods/services and a much larger gasoline shock make inflation persistence more credible than an isolated August setback, without proving a self-sustaining domestic price spiral.

Context from prior regional live file: July CPI showed +0.2% monthly core and restrained shelter; August partly reversed stabilization through non-housing services and fuel. September extends that reversal with broader core momentum and stronger petroleum-cost transmission.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: CPI sharply strengthens the inflation case for additional restriction, but the distinction between October timing and cumulative policy is essential. September FOMC had raised the policy range to 3.75–4.00%; speaker communication favored patience rather than automatic consecutive hikes.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: Repeated core +0.3% and stronger non-housing services favor the hawkish case, yet direct gasoline effects, subdued primary rents and real-income compression argue against conflating price pressure with sustainable excess demand. Verified immediate market reaction was front-end-led and USD-positive, but not evidence of a settled October FOMC decision.

What to verify next: Core PCE based on CPI/PPI components, supercore composition, subsequent inflation expectations, retailer control/real PCE and whether fuel/travel prices normalize. Monitor FOMC communication for genuine earlier-tightening language.

Macro configuration: petroleum shock + higher underlying CPI momentum + selective services/goods breadth + weaker real wages + contested October policy timing.

THURSDAY 15 OCT 2026

UNITED STATES — NY FED EMPIRE STATE MANUFACTURING SURVEY (Oct)

Release Date: 15 Oct 2026 | Local Time: 14:30 (Paris)
Importance: ***

PM FLASH: Empire State surged to 25.5 from 7.6 (10.25 poll), with new orders 23.2 and shipments 13.1; supply availability deteriorated and selling-price diffusion rose.

PM READ-THROUGH: The October rebound is confirmed by orders, not merely sentiment, but capacity bottlenecks, muted hiring acceleration and weaker six-month optimism limit extrapolation to national manufacturing.

PM DEBATE & KEY TAKEAWAYS: Professional insight: Empire’s strong orders conflict with Philadelphia’s order slump in the same release window. Both show firmer selling-price diffusion. Later national orders and output must establish whether this is regional dispersion or a durable factory recovery. Regional diffusion is not a substitute for national hard output.

1. Reuters Data

NY Fed Manufacturing: 25,50 | Prior: 7,60 | Poll: 10,25 | Surprise: 15,250

2. Professional Market Commentary

The survey was interpreted as a pronounced manufacturing activity and orders rebound: its general conditions index reached the highest since December 2021. Barron’s emphasized the near-five-year headline and improved orders; Investing.com juxtaposed it with the negative Philadelphia surprise. The official survey showed higher backlogs, slower delivery times, worsening supply availability, modest positive hiring and higher selling-price diffusion despite slightly easing input-price diffusion. Six-month business expectations declined from a positive level.

No independent named bank economist with a separately differentiated view was established; no Tier-1 research disagreement was verified. Empire was released at exactly the same time as Philadelphia, PPI, Retail Sales and weekly claims, with opposite regional surprises. No Empire-specific rates, FX or equity move is attributable.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment

This is genuine regional order-flow improvement following weak September orders and shipments, but evidence is insufficient for a national manufacturing acceleration. Supply constraints may inflate backlogs and delivery times; labor intensity and expectations do not corroborate the headline's magnitude.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms

Activity and orders (Sep → Oct): General conditions 7.6 → 25.5 (+17.9); new orders 2.0 → 23.2 (+21.2); shipments -3.2 → 13.1 (+16.3); unfilled orders 5.9 → 14.0 (+8.1). Inventories improved. The headline is a standalone diffusion question, not a production-weighted percentage growth measure.

Supply and backlogs. Supply availability fell to -15.1, its weakest since June 2022; delivery times reached 19.8. Orders and shipments confirm demand improvement, but backlogs and longer deliveries can reflect shortages and expensive transport rather than fully deliverable output. Survey fieldwork occurred 2–9 October, before the CPI/PPI releases.

Labor and forward expectations. Employment +10.3 versus +10.6 in September; workweek +9.1 versus +17.0. Hiring remained positive but did not accelerate alongside orders. Six-month general conditions declined to 21.0 from 29.0; future supply availability weakened, price expectations strengthened and capex intentions remained modest. Lower optimism does not equal an expected contraction.

Pricing. Prices Paid eased 63.1 → 59.5 yet remained high; Prices Received rose 28.1 → 30.6. More firms raising output prices despite some easing in input-price diffusion supports selective cost transmission, but diffusion indexes do not measure price magnitude or margins.

National corroboration challenge. September manufacturing output increased +0.3% m/m while Q3 factory growth slowed to +0.7% annualized. Philadelphia shows opposing current orders and delivery-time behavior; only October national ISM/orders and actual production can discriminate between regional volatility and broad stabilization.

C. State Transition & Historical Context

State transition: reversal — September’s regional order and shipment weakness turns into a strong October rebound, but price/supply friction and weaker future optimism prevent a broad durable-acceleration conclusion.

Context from prior regional live file: August Empire showed strong activity before September softened markedly; October reverses current order and shipment weakness while intensifying supply availability pressure and selling-price diffusion.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: A positive early-Q4 manufacturing orders signal counterbalances weak Q3 factory momentum, reducing the risk of imminent industrial contraction without proving national overheating.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: When higher orders coexist with supply bottlenecks, faster backlog growth may be real demand, delayed fulfillment or both. Philadelphia’s simultaneously weaker orders and broadly rising output-price diffusion illustrate the danger of making national growth/rates calls from one volatile regional survey. The release alone cannot identify a market reaction.

What to verify next: October ISM Manufacturing orders/production/prices; national manufacturing output, equipment and industrial diffusion; other regional supply-availability and delivery-time measures.

Macro configuration: strong regional orders + slower fulfillment + modest positive employment + broader selling prices + softer medium-term confidence.

UNITED STATES — PHILADELPHIA FED MANUFACTURING BUSINESS OUTLOOK SURVEY (Oct)

Release Date: 15 Oct 2026 | Local Time: 14:30 (Paris)
Importance: ***

PM FLASH: Philadelphia Fed fell to 20.9 from 37.8 (28.4 poll); new orders plunged to 4.3, while prices received rose to 40.1 despite slowing shipments.

PM READ-THROUGH: Positive headline activity masks a sharp loss of order breadth and future optimism. More widespread selling-price increases without stronger demand preserve an adverse inflation/growth mix.

PM DEBATE & KEY TAKEAWAYS: Professional insight: Current deceleration contrasts with Empire’s simultaneous rebound, while planned 2027 capex remains constructive. The crucial test is whether national manufacturing orders track Philadelphia or Empire, and whether pricing diffusion persists as delivery delays recede. Positive capex intentions do not yet prove realized spending.

1. Reuters Data

Philly Fed Business Indx: 20,9 | Prior: 37,8 | Poll: 28,4 | Surprise: -7,50

2. Professional Market Commentary

The official Philadelphia Fed tape describes expansion that is positive but much less widespread, with weak new orders, moderating shipments, workweek and backlogs, yet firmer selling prices. Kitco emphasized the headline miss against expectations and continued expansion; the Philadelphia Fed highlighted high prices and weakening future indicators. No independent named bank economist interpretation was verified, so a manufactured professional bull/bear split would be inappropriate.

The special annual capital-expenditure question showed more than half of respondents intending to raise total 2027 expenditure, a constructive medium-term counter-signal. The 08:30 ET release coincided with Empire, PPI, retail and claims. Kitco reported gold around $4,154 (+1.2% during coverage), but no bond/USD/gold move can be assigned specifically to Philadelphia.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment

Philadelphia manufacturing remains in expansion but is experiencing material loss of order-flow momentum, weakening workweeks and future expectations. More firms simultaneously report increasing selling prices. The signal is slower regional demand with inflation transmission pressure, not a generalized factory contraction.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms

Current diffusion (Sep → Oct): general activity 37.8 → 20.9 (-16.9); new orders 29.2 → 4.3 (-24.9); shipments 27.7 → 15.3 (-12.4); unfilled orders 20.4 → 2.4 (-18.0); delivery times 26.5 → 8.5 (-18.0); inventories -12.5 → -12.8. August's headline was 47.4, so this is a two-month narrowing. Order shares: 38.5% increasing, 34.1% decreasing, 21.7% unchanged; the balance measures diffusion, not a 25% volume collapse.

Labor and utilization. Employment 11.8 → 9.1 and workweek 18.0 → 7.5, lowest since June. Employment respondents: 18.0% increasing, 8.8% decreasing, 67.6% unchanged. Labor absorption remains positive but operating intensity is weakening, consistent with caution and potential labor hoarding rather than job cuts already underway.

Inflation and supply. Prices Paid eased 48.6 → 43.2, while Prices Received increased 31.3 → 40.1, the highest since May 2025; selling-price increases were reported by 41.1% of firms against 33% previously. Future Prices Paid 71.3 → 62.9, Future Prices Received 72.3 → 62.1. Slower delivery-time and unfilled-order diffusion contrasts with Empire's supply tightening. Lower supplier delays could reflect improved supply or weaker orders; simultaneous order declines support an underlying activity slowdown. Price diffusion neither identifies average percentage increases nor confirms rising profits.

Outlook. Six-month general conditions 52.9 → 33.0; future new orders 62.3 → 37.0; shipments 61.1 → 35.2; employment 50.6 → 30.1; capex 37.1 → 34.9. All remain positive but considerably weaker. Annual 2027 spending intentions: 52.2% expect higher total capex, 47.8% unchanged, none lower, versus 36% higher and 19% lower a year earlier. Breakdown: noncomputer equipment 50% higher; software and computer hardware 39.1%; structures 34.8%. Intentions are not realized expenditure and the special-question sample need not equal the main panel.

Cross-regional and national comparison. Empire new orders and shipments rebound sharply while Philadelphia weakens; both see higher selling-price diffusion and weaker future optimism. They cannot be averaged mechanically across distinct samples. September national factory +0.3% and Q3 +0.7% annualized suggest a national stabilization without convincing broad acceleration.

C. State Transition & Historical Context

State transition: deterioration — after exceptional August conditions, orders approach neutral, workweek and forward expectations weaken, but selling-price diffusion continues rising despite slower activity.

Context from prior regional live file: August Philadelphia showed exceptional manufacturing breadth; September normalized the peak with rising cost pressure. October extends the order/workweek slowdown while broadening prices received, without a general activity contraction.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: Philadelphia adds growth-side caution and simultaneously preserves the producer-price constraint. The 2027 capex-intentions balance is a meaningful long-horizon offset but no proof of delivered investment.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: If national orders follow Philadelphia, weaker industrial demand would moderate urgency for additional restriction; if Empire leads, a stronger manufacturing rebound remains plausible. Persistent selling-price diffusion during order weakness creates margin and stagflation risk with ambiguous front-end rate implications. The combined 15 October market window cannot support release-specific attribution.

What to verify next: October national ISM orders/prices, industrial output and workweeks; other regional surveys; realized investment relative to 2027 intentions; output-price persistence as deliveries normalize.

Macro configuration: slower regional orders + positive but diminishing activity/hiring + weaker six-month outlook + rising selling-price breadth + prospective capital investment resilience.

UNITED STATES — PPI FINAL DEMAND / CORE PPI / MACHINE MANUFACTURING (Sep)

Release Date: 15 Oct 2026 | Local Time: 14:30 (Paris)
Importance: ****

PM FLASH: PPI jumped 1.3% m/m versus 0.5% expected; ex-food/energy rose 0.7% versus 0.3%. Fuel drove goods, but trade margins and freight also accelerated.

PM READ-THROUGH: Producer inflation extends August’s energy shock into services margins, transportation and ex-food/energy/trade prices; preliminary PCE components imply renewed underlying consumer-price persistence.

PM DEBATE & KEY TAKEAWAYS: Debate: Strong wholesale inflation raised the case for earlier tightening, but weak retail control and cautious Fed signals still favored a possible October pause. Key takeaways: Separate trade-margin volatility from ex-trade core and determine whether upstream diesel costs reach final consumers.

1. Reuters Data

PPI Machine Manuf'ing: 200,1 | Prior: 199,5 | Revised: 199,7

PPI Final Demand YY: 6,3% | Prior: 5,4% | Revised: 5,6% | Poll: 5,3% | Surprise: 1,00%

PPI Final Demand MM: 1,3% | Prior: 0,4% | Revised: 0,5% | Poll: 0,5% | Surprise: 0,80%

PPI exFood/Energy YY: 5,0% | Prior: 4,6% | Revised: 4,8% | Poll: 4,4% | Surprise: 0,60%

PPI exFood/Energy MM: 0,7% | Prior: 0,2% | Poll: 0,3% | Surprise: 0,40%

2. Professional Market Commentary

Institutional commentary called this a second major inflation surprise following CPI. Final-demand goods surged due to gasoline and diesel, but the professional emphasis was stronger services PPI, trade margins, freight and core-PCE feeder categories. Reuters cited market core-PCE estimates around +0.31–0.36% m/m / 3.1% y/y and drew attention to weaker underlying retail control despite nominal headline spending.

Matthew Martin (Oxford Economics) argued a still-solid labor market and persistent prices made October tightening defensible. Stephen Brown (Capital Economics) estimated roughly 0.35% core PCE and judged October somewhat more likely after PPI, conditional on financial conditions. Chris Zaccarelli (Northlight) agreed further 2026 tightening was likely but expected the Fed to wait until December. Chris Osmond (Fifth Third) highlighted inflation and consumption strength alongside weaker labor momentum. Mark Streiber (FHN Financial) emphasized trade-margin pass-through; Oren Klachkin (Nationwide) cited the consecutive price surprises and potential AI-related pressures. The communicated patience of Williams, Jefferson and Goolsbee conflicted with treating the release as a standalone October trigger.

Reuters reported lower Treasury yields and a softer USD during the combined 15 October data window despite the PPI upside; October hike odds remained around 30% in one reported observation. Reuters described equities higher at one timestamp, Yahoo Finance mixed indexes and Nasdaq weakness at another. These are non-identical intraday observations. PPI, retail, claims and regional surveys shared the same 08:30 ET timestamp, so no isolated PPI reaction is established.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment

Wholesale price acceleration extends beyond direct energy into distribution margins, freight and selected PCE-relevant services. Yet the largest aggregates remain heavily energy- and trade-margin-sensitive; the economic issue is whether non-energy costs and producer price-setting translate into sustained consumer inflation, particularly while retail-control demand decelerates.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms

Headline and revisions. Final-demand PPI +1.3% m/m and +6.3% y/y after August revised +0.5% / +5.6%, not a rebound from a benign prior month. July/August/September sequence: headline +0.2/+0.5/+1.3%; goods -0.4/+1.1/+2.6%; services +0.2/+0.2/+0.8%; excluding food/energy/trade +0.5/+0.3/+0.5%.

Goods and energy. Final goods +2.6%, largest gain in the series dating from December 2009. Energy +10.8% explained over 80% of that increase; gasoline +20.3% supplied approximately half of total goods inflation. Diesel and jet fuel sharply higher; food +1.2% after three consecutive declines. Goods excluding food/energy +0.3%, slower than August’s +0.4%, preventing a generalized non-energy goods-breakout inference. Diesel’s 21.0% rise matters for agriculture, freight, distribution and processed goods.

Services and margins. Final services +0.8% after +0.2%; trade-service margins +1.4% accounted for nearly half; transport/warehousing +3.4%; services excluding trade, transport and warehousing +0.3%. Machinery/vehicle wholesaling margins +3.9% explained over 20% of the total services increase; trucking +3.8%, lodging +5.6% and airline passenger services +5.0%. Auto fuel retail margins fell 30.3%, underscoring unequal distribution pricing. PPI trade services measure *changes in retail/wholesale distribution margins*, not aggregate company profitability or automatic CPI pass-through.

Core definitions. Conventional ex-food/energy PPI +0.7% m/m / +5.0% y/y versus +0.2% prior; excluding food, energy and trade services +0.5% / +5.0%, versus +0.3% prior. Removing trade margins reduces the extraordinary monthly reading but leaves an uncomfortable underlying acceleration.

Intermediate pipeline. Processed goods +2.5% m/m / +14.1% y/y, unprocessed +8.4% / +21.5%, intermediate services +0.9% / +6.3%, processed energy goods +10.2%. Production stages: Stage 1 +2.2% / +13.5%; Stage 2 +3.9% / +13.9%; Stage 3 +1.1% / +7.7%; Stage 4 +1.1% / +7.9%. These reveal exposure, not one-to-one future CPI changes; fuel drives much of their scale.

PCE bridge. PCE-relevant airline passenger services +5.0%, traveler accommodation +5.6%, legal services +0.3%, while securities brokerage/investment advice declined. Economists' September core PCE estimates +0.31–0.36% m/m, near 3.1% y/y versus 3.0% in August. This is provisional; BEA weights and classifications differ from PPI.

Demand check. Simultaneous retail headline +0.8% but control +0.1% versus +0.3% poll, together with energy-led real-wage erosion, argue against inferring domestic demand overheating from inflation alone. Claims 199k indicate no acute layoff shock, not evidence of rapidly rising payrolls. Claims was not built as an independent release block.

C. State Transition & Historical Context

State transition: deterioration — August’s mainly fuel/intermediate producer shock extends into higher trade margins, transport services and firmer ex-food/energy/trade PPI, while generalized consumer-price transmission remains unproven.

Context from prior regional live file: June–July enjoyed energy-led producer disinflation; August reversed via fuel and intermediate goods but retained relatively restrained trade margins. September adds distribution/freight and ex-trade core increases to that established pipeline shock.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: PPI materially raises confidence that the hotter CPI belongs to a wider inflation deterioration; the preferred Fed PCE measure may also accelerate. The implication is stronger pressure for additional tightening, not automatic October action.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: Wholesale energy and freight feed intermediate stages, but distribution margins can reverse and real consumption may weaken before full pass-through. October timing depends on Fed communication, labor and financial conditions; December later-tightening baseline still coherent. The simultaneous release cluster prevents assigning lower yields/USD to PPI alone.

What to verify next: Official September core PCE and service components, October ex-trade core PPI, transport/trade margins, retail control and household real-income trends.

Macro configuration: reinforcing CPI/PPI inflation + large energy inputs + firmer margins/logistics + provisional hot core PCE + uncertain demand transmission.

UNITED STATES — RETAIL SALES / EX-AUTOS / RETAIL CONTROL (Sep)

Release Date: 15 Oct 2026 | Local Time: 14:30 (Paris)

PM FLASH: Headline retail sales rose 0.8% versus 0.3% expected, but gasoline generated over 70% of the gain; retail control rose only 0.1% versus 0.3%.

PM READ-THROUGH: The nominal headline beat masks almost flat estimated real retail activity and narrower spending breadth; robust Q3 consumption survives, but an energy-led Q4 household squeeze becomes more plausible.

PM DEBATE & KEY TAKEAWAYS: Debate: Is +0.1% control an early real-demand deterioration or payback after exceptionally strong August? Key takeaways: Gas-station receipts rose 6.4% while ex-gasoline sales barely grew; historical benchmark revisions weaken the previously assumed consumer baseline. Retail-price deflators and services spending remain necessary cross-checks.

1. Reuters Data

Retail Sales MM: 0,8% | Prior: 1,2% | Revised: 1,3% | Poll: 0,3% | Surprise: 0,50%

Retail Sales Ex-Autos MM: 0,9% | Prior: 1,4% | Revised: 1,4% | Poll: 0,5% | Surprise: 0,40%

Retail Control: 0,1% | Prior: 1,4% | Revised: 1,2% | Poll: 0,3% | Surprise: -0,20%

2. Professional Market Commentary

Institutional commentary agreed that gasoline prices exaggerated nominal headline strength but differed on the durability of the slowdown. Michael Pearce (Oxford Economics) expected the oil-driven income squeeze to lower spending into the holiday season; Natalie Kotlyar (BDO) emphasized savings, promotions and rising margin pressure. Eliza Winger (Bloomberg Economics, via TheStreet Pro) viewed September control as normalization after exceptional August, rather than demand collapse. Gregory Daco and Lydia Boussour (EY-Parthenon, relayed) highlighted continuing resilience despite inflation. Ksenia Bushmeneva (TD Economics) estimated around +0.1% real retail growth; Michael Bazdarich (Western Asset) estimated nominal control about +0.15% versus control-related prices +0.20%, suggesting marginally negative real control but a still-positive trend. Reuters noted stronger higher-income spending than lower-income demand.

The September 28 Census benchmark revision substantially altered historical retail levels. No independent retail-specific market reaction can be isolated: release coincided with PPI, claims and regional factory surveys; post-release lower yields and softer USD were combined-window observations.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment

The headline beat is compositionally weak, with most nominal spending growth coming from gasoline rather than increasing real purchases. Control-group and real-sales calculations suggest a genuine loss of September marginal momentum without overturning relatively robust Q3 growth. The evidence supports an adverse nominal-real divergence, not established total-household-consumption contraction.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms

Headline and gasoline. Total sales $745.0bn, +0.8% m/m and +6.3% y/y; August revised +1.3%. September versus August: headline +0.8/+1.3%, ex-autos +0.9/+1.4%, ex-gas +0.2/+1.0%, ex-autos/ex-gas +0.2/+1.1%, retail control +0.1/+1.2%. Gasoline stations +6.4% m/m and +28.1% y/y. TheStreet Pro estimated 0.55pp of the unrounded 0.77% headline gain came from gas, more than 70%. Census reported ex-autos/ex-gas change statistically indistinguishable from zero at 90% confidence. Gasoline receipts rise with price even if volumes stagnate.

Control and quarterly arithmetic. Control +0.1% versus +0.3% poll after August revised from +1.4% to +1.2%. Excludes autos, gas, construction materials and restaurants; more useful for BEA goods consumption than headline receipts. Nominal control quarterly annualization: Q2 about +7.37%, Q3 +4.27%; September control level +4.64% y/y. Deceleration from a strong base is not yet contraction.

Category breadth. Eight of 13 categories rose versus 13 in August. Furniture +1.3%; electronics +0.6%; health/personal care +0.7%; food/beverage +0.4%; nonstores +0.3% versus +2.0% August; autos +0.2%; restaurants +1.1% m/m / +7.0% y/y. Weakness: miscellaneous -3.0%, building materials -0.6%, sporting goods/hobby/books -0.5%, general merchandise -0.1%, clothing unchanged. Discretionary demand is mixed rather than universally weak.

Real deflation. TD estimated real retail +0.1%, TheStreet Pro +0.12%. Western Asset estimated control nominal about +0.15% versus control-prices +0.20%, implying slightly negative real control. These are analyst deflations, not BEA real PCE; headline CPI is not a correct retail basket deflator and services dominate total household spending. Consistent with real hourly earnings -0.5% m/m / -0.7% y/y.

Benchmark revisions. Census September 28 historical benchmark incorporated 2023–24 annual survey corrections. TheStreet Pro estimated a ~4.5% lower historical sales level, with revised growth: 2023 1.39% (prior 3.53%), 2024 1.05% (prior 2.62%), 2025 3.51% (prior 3.95%). Western Asset noted significant 2022–24 control changes, January 2026 and pharmacy-series revisions and a mismatch with BEA pharmaceutical expenditures. Avoid mechanically mixing pre-/post-revision data.

Q3 versus Q4. Institutional Q3 real consumption tracking remained Oxford Economics +3.3%, Reuters economist estimates +3.4%, TD +3.6% annualized versus about +3.8% in Q2. Restaurant/service demand remains positive and MARTS does not capture total PCE. The key hypothesis is that September begins oil-induced demand weakening; another month and real PCE are needed before calling a regime break.

C. State Transition & Historical Context

State transition: deterioration in monthly momentum / stabilization at the quarterly level — September reverses August’s broad-based rebound and concentrates nominal growth in gasoline, but robust Q3 consumption limits the structural-downturn inference.

Context from prior regional live file: July retail weakness was partly promotional timing; August’s broad rebound restored near-term resilience. September control and category breadth weaken, while the Q3 level remains supportive and higher energy expenses create new forward pressure.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: This is the central growth-side qualification to the hawkish CPI/PPI tape. Weak control and real purchasing power reduce urgency for additional restriction while robust Q3 spending and low layoffs limit an easing argument.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: An oil shock raises nominal fuel spending but absorbs real household income; subsequent demand destruction is conditional on services consumption and labor income. Analysts disagree whether September is August payback or a Q4 slowdown starting point. Do not double-count the 15 October combined-market move as a unique retail reaction.

What to verify next: September real PCE/personal income, October control and spending breadth, household credit/savings, lower-income demand and wages, service consumption.

Macro configuration: gasoline-led nominal strength + near-flat real sales + control miss + narrower retail breadth + still-strong Q3 consumption.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment

September amplifies an existing August nonfuel import-cost shock with renewed fuel inflation, worsening producer and investment-goods cost conditions. The consumer-price implications require differentiation among industrial inputs, imported capital goods and directly consumed goods, as well as absorption through pricing and margins.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms

Headline progression. Import prices +1.1% m/m vs +0.8% expected; +8.1% y/y versus revised +6.7%. August revised from +0.7% to +0.5%. July/August/September: all imports -0.4/+0.5/+1.1%; fuel -6.8/-0.2/+4.8%; nonfuel +0.3/+0.6/+0.7%. Nonfuel +6.0% y/y, highest since April 2022, with no monthly decline since August 2025.

Unresolved pass-through. Nonfuel import strength and capital-goods pricing weaken the external disinflation buffer but do not establish a full consumer-price spiral. Factory spare capacity may permit cost absorption, with possible profit compression or slower output if energy prices persist.

C. State Transition & Historical Context

State transition: continuation of deterioration — August nonfuel import-price pressure persists and September adds renewed imported energy inflation, intensifying external pipeline risk before completed final-consumer transmission.

Context from prior regional live file: June–July external price relief reversed in August through nonfuel materials and capital goods despite falling fuel. September retains that nonfuel impulse and adds energy, with revised August nonfuel still robust at +0.6%.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: Broader traded-goods pricing strengthens the inflation constraint beyond domestic CPI/PPI, especially equipment/industrial costs. It contributes little independently to the October FOMC timing debate.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: Tariffs are outside import-price indexes and AI demand can boost imported investment prices without raising domestic production; the Fed cannot directly reverse a petroleum/supply shortage, although it can restrain pass-through. A rising import-price index is not identical to realized household inflation.

What to verify next: October nonfuel ex-food/fuel imports, CPI core goods, imported machinery versus US equipment output, corporate margins and oil/freight durability.

C. State Transition & Historical Context

State transition: stabilization after August deterioration — positive monthly factory growth returns, but Q3 manufacturing loses substantial momentum and high-tech/utilities strength masks weak activity elsewhere.

Context from prior regional live file: July factory activity indicated modest stabilization; August interrupted it through equipment/durable weakness. September reverses the monthly loss but fails to restore Q2’s broader factory momentum; utilization remains subdued.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: IP supports the economy's ability to avoid near-term factory contraction, not a compelling demand-driven overheating case. The Fed can maintain restriction but the headline alone does not justify more aggressive tightening.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: Higher imported industrial input costs occur despite significant domestic factory slack, creating margin, price and demand trade-offs. Narrow semiconductor production and utility strength can mislead investors extrapolating broad industrial acceleration, while import-intensive AI capex limits US manufacturing spillovers.

What to verify next: October national factory output excluding utilities and high tech; ISM orders versus realized production; equipment output versus imported hardware; vehicles, capacity utilization and the November 24 benchmark revision.

Macro configuration: monthly industrial rebound + utilities/high-tech concentration + slowing factory quarterly trend + spare utilization + rising imported-cost pressure.

D. CENTRAL BANK TAPE

Federal Reserve — Speaker Scout v2.0
Window: 4–17 October 2026
Policy reference: Fed funds target range 3.75–4.00%, following the unanimous 25bp increase on 16 September. Next FOMC: 27–28 October. Blackout begins 17 October.

Summary — Policy reaction function

Dominant signal: further tightening remains the committee's central expectation, but October is not the preferred timing; the terminal policy rate is more contested than the next meeting.

The 7 October FOMC minutes establish that most participants expected another hike before year-end, while several considered policy accommodative or only mildly restrictive. Waller's 8 October intervention is the defining communication: additional hikes are consistent with the projected rate path without requiring consecutive moves. Williams, Bowman and Daly reinforce patience, while Collins supports another 2026 increase without selecting October. The hawkish flank, especially Hammack and Musalem, sees insufficient restriction and potentially more cumulative tightening.

The 14 October CPI surprise increases the inflation-side pressure but does not visibly dislodge the committee's patient center. Goolsbee shifts conditionally hawkish, Hammack emphasizes inflation psychology and Daly explicitly maintains that the committee has time. Warsh's 16 October refusal to prejudge meetings provides no new commitment and reinforces the no-forward-guidance approach. This is a conditional hawkish hold, not a dovish turn: postponing the next move is consistent with further tightening, while the split over whether one additional hike is sufficient remains unresolved.

FOMC Minutes — 7 October 2026
Importance: ****
Meeting covered: 15–16 September 2026. Official FOMC minutes; high-confidence primary source.
Key policy signal:
All voting participants supported September's 25bp hike. Most participants assessed that another increase would likely be appropriate before year-end, although each meeting would be approached with an open mind. Almost all judged labor-market risks to be broadly balanced and inflation risks tilted upward. Several considered existing monetary policy not restrictive, or only mildly so. A minority raised the prospect of a higher neutral rate.
Representative quote:
“would likely be appropriate by year end”
Incremental reaction function:
The minutes establish the committee-wide rationale for additional tightening rather than assigning that view to individual speakers. They support the December-hike baseline but do not lock October out. The relevant uncertainty is whether the still-accommodative-policy assessment implies a higher eventual destination, or principally the completion of the rate adjustment already signaled.

Christopher Waller — Fed Governor, voter — 8 October 2026
Importance: ****
Istanbul Economic Forum, Central Bank of Türkiye. Official Federal Reserve text; high confidence.
Key policy signal:
Expects additional rate increases if the data develop as projected, explicitly separating cumulative tightening from its calendar pace. Notes that 16 of 18 September SEP participants expected at least one further hike during 2026, with four expecting two. Identifies the Middle East energy shock, AI-related technology prices and renewed tariff threats as inflation risks; considers the labor market sufficiently stable to prioritize inflation. Does not push back against the futures-implied tightening path cited in the speech.
Representative quote:
“The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings”
Incremental reaction function:
A material clarification of the September hike: policy reflects cumulative inflation evidence, not one month's CPI data, and tightening need not occur at back-to-back meetings. Strong evidence for an October skip remaining compatible with a hawkish eventual rate path. Inflation expectations are the central risk threshold; growth damage from incremental restriction is not his principal concern.

No new meeting-specific rate signal. His description of September as removing accommodation leaves uncertainty over whether he sees substantially more cumulative tightening ahead. The Chair's silence must not be transformed mechanically into an October-hold commitment.

Human voice — institutional interpretation

Jan Hatzius — Goldman Sachs, 16 October: Reads Warsh's remarks and broader FOMC communications as consistent with an October pause followed by a second and final hike in December. This is not official guidance.
Jeff Schulze — Franklin Templeton Institute, 14 October: Hot inflation strengthens the case for later tightening but “the bar is high for an immediate hike.”
Christopher Hodge — Natixis, 14 October: Before CPI, expected a December final hike absent core CPI around 0.4%; actual +0.3% did not reach that threshold.
Sam Williamson — First American Financial, 14 October: Counter-view that broad inflation could justify advancing the December hike to October.
Institutional endpoint disagreement: Williams and relayed JPM Asset Management expect one more then extended pause; relayed Bloomberg Economics expects no further 2026 hike and a 2027 cut; Hammack/hawkish flank and a share of SEP dots prefer more. Aggregator-only economist reports remain lower-confidence than official text.

Bottom line — central bank tape

Policy bias: Conditional hawkish hold, with additional 2026 tightening favored but no clear committee commitment to October.
Next-meeting center: October pause / December hike, supported by Waller's timing flexibility, Williams' one-more-hike view, Bowman's patience, Daly's post-CPI comments and Warsh's refusal to push for an earlier move.
Hawkish tail: Hammack's insufficient-restriction assessment and the FOMC minutes' higher-neutral-rate discussion keep additional increases beyond December plausible.
Policy destination: Substantially less settled than the next meeting. Williams sees little justification for additional 2027 increases, while the hawkish flank and part of the SEP support a higher endpoint.
Reaction function: Further broadening of core-services inflation, inflation expectations and realized demand strength would increase pressure to tighten sooner or further. Slowing real consumption, weak hiring and financial tightening would support a longer pause, particularly if energy-related inflation begins fading.
Evidence limits: The full Warsh transcript, original Hammack Barron's interview, parts of Bowman's Q&A and several lower-confidence speaker reports were unavailable. Jefferson, Barr, Paulson, Powell and several other voters provided no verified new in-window policy views. The apparent committee center is therefore well supported directionally, but not established through a complete contemporaneous voter poll.
Final interpretation: The CPI/PPI shock made further tightening more compelling, but the Fed deliberately preserved discretion over October. The relevant distinction for rates and FX is between higher-for-longer or a higher terminal rate and an immediate consecutive hike. The tape supports the former more confidently than the latter.

E. SIGNAL TENSION CHECK

Main contradiction:
The release tape shows intensifying core and upstream inflation despite weaker retail-control momentum, subdued realized hiring and substantial industrial slack. The Fed speaker tape adds a second dimension to that contradiction: a broad tightening bias coexists with a committee center reluctant to accelerate the next hike, while hawks question whether policy is sufficiently restrictive at all.

Why it matters:
The Fed must distinguish persistent domestic inflation and renewed pricing power from supply-driven inflation that may weaken real demand. That distinction governs both the urgency of the October decision and the terminal-rate debate.

Implication:
October hold / December hike remains the communication-consistent baseline, but persistent core inflation with resilient realized demand would challenge the pause. Conversely, further consumption and employment deterioration would weaken the case for a higher terminal even if headline inflation stays elevated.

F. 5 KEY RELEASES TO DIG INTO

**** CPI / Core CPI / CPI-W (14 Oct)
Why it matters: Core CPI +0.3% m/m for a second month, with a +0.1pp upside surprise and 3m annualized momentum of approximately 3.4%. Energy dominates headline inflation, but stronger core goods and non-energy services raise the persistence risk. The pivotal question is whether the acceleration survives in services excluding energy and shelter.

**** PPI / Core PPI (15 Oct)
Why it matters: Final-demand PPI +1.3% versus +0.5% expected and conventional core +0.7% versus +0.3%. Trade margins, freight, non-energy producer pricing and PCE-relevant services provide the strongest additional evidence of upstream-to-downstream transmission. Distinguishing volatile margins from persistent underlying inflation is crucial.

*** ISM Services PMI (5 Oct)
Why it matters: Prices Paid at 74.0, the highest since July 2022, alongside New Orders at 59.8. The report captures the Fed's most important growth/inflation dilemma: continued services demand and exceptionally widespread cost pressure despite moderating current activity and only marginal employment expansion.

*** Retail Sales / Retail Control (15 Oct)
Why it matters: Headline sales +0.8% versus +0.3% expected conceal retail control of only +0.1% versus +0.3%. Gasoline explains more than 70% of nominal headline growth, while estimated real retail demand is approximately flat. This is the principal counterweight to the domestic-overheating interpretation and an early test of energy-driven demand destruction.

*** S&P Global Services / Composite PMI Final (5 Oct)
Why it matters: Services at 58.8, a five-year high, supported by strong domestic new business, hiring diffusion and backlog accumulation. Its activity and employment signals are materially stronger than ISM and realized payroll data, while its inflation measures independently corroborate the later CPI/PPI deterioration. Determining whether this measures durable real demand or diffusion amplified by capacity constraints is central to the policy assessment.

G. RED TEAM QUESTIONS

1. Inflation persistence versus energy pass-through: Will realized September core PCE and subsequent services prices confirm broad inflation beyond energy, travel, shelter and volatile PPI trade margins?
2. Policy timing versus terminal: Does the combination of hot CPI/PPI and the minutes' assessment of insufficient restriction imply merely one delayed hike, or is Williams' expectation of no additional 2027 tightening too dovish?
3. October policy threshold: What observable combination of core inflation, realized hiring and consumption resilience would be sufficient to overcome the wait-and-assess position expressed by Waller, Williams, Bowman and Daly?
4. Consumer-demand falsification: Does September retail control +0.1% represent the first stage of an inflation-driven Q4 consumption slowdown, or only normalization after August's unusually strong rebound?
5. Labor-market contradiction: Why does S&P report exceptionally strong services hiring diffusion while ISM employment remains near neutral and realized payroll growth is subdued? Which indicator better reflects the labor-market conditions informing the FOMC?
6. Manufacturing and AI transmission: Will national orders and production confirm Empire's rebound or Philadelphia's slowdown? Could strong AI investment raise imported input prices and inflation without materially improving broader domestic capacity utilization?
7. Communication reliability: Does Warsh's refusal to guide leave the FOMC's actual October decision more open than external economists suggest, especially given the absence of verified in-window remarks from several voting members?

H. CURRENCY MARKET-CONSENSUS SCAN

Bottom line

Pair convention: EUR/USD — lower EUR/USD means a stronger USD. At the beginning of the data window, the public institutional consensus remained moderately bearish USD over a 6–12 month horizon, despite the dollar's powerful September rally. The Reuters survey conducted 30 September–2 October, covering nearly 70 FX strategists, projected EUR/USD at 1.14 in one month, 1.15 in three and six months, and 1.16 in twelve months. However, 80% of respondents who assessed near-term forecast risks thought the dollar was more likely to outperform their three-month projections than underperform. The defining starting configuration was therefore medium-term dollar bearishness with increasingly uncomfortable near-term USD upside risk. Source: Reuters FX poll, 2 October, https://www.reuters.com/business/us-dollar-strength-fizzle-fx-forecasters-unmoved-by-searing-rally-2026-10-02/

During the window, the tactical public-bank view moved further toward USD resilience. MUFG's October outlook projected EUR/USD at 1.12 for Q4, below the 1.16 consensus benchmark shown in its forecast table, while ING's 12–13 October revision placed EUR/USD at 1.13 for Q4 and Q1 2027 and emphasized downside risk toward 1.11. Commerzbank's previously revised 1.15 year-end target provided a less dollar-bullish reference. This was not a wholesale reversal of the Reuters survey's longer-horizon weak-dollar call: rather, near-term bank forecasts and tactical commentary became more cautious about fighting USD strength. Sources: https://www.mufgresearch.com/fx/monthly-foreign-exchange-outlook-october-2026 ; https://think.ing.com/articles/g10-fx-talking-october-2026/ ; https://www.fxstreet.com/news/euro-credibility-restored-supports-dollar-commerzbank-202609251336

Price action exposed the distinction. EUR/USD fell to approximately 1.1113 on 14 October following the CPI shock, while DXY reached an 18-month high near 102.94 intraday. By 16 October, EUR/USD had recovered toward 1.1250 and DXY had retreated to approximately 101.87 as Treasury yields declined, October Fed-hike expectations faded and AI-related financial-market concerns complicated the dollar's rate advantage. The dollar still traded stronger than the median survey's projected EUR/USD levels, but spot was no longer moving one-way toward the most USD-bullish tactical forecasts. Sources: https://www.marketscreener.com/news/dollar-hits-18-month-high-then-cools-as-investors-await-patient-fed-ce785dd2d089f123 ; https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/euro-gets-much-needed-reprieve-ai-wobbles-rock-dollar-2026-10-16/

Consensus at window close: The market retained a structural divide between the survey's medium-term expectation of USD depreciation and a more USD-supportive near-term institutional framework based on Fed credibility, rate differentials, US growth resilience, oil and European fiscal stress. The 16 October reversal weakened the tactical asymmetry for chasing dollar strength after a substantial rally; it did not demonstrate that the broader weak-dollar forecast had been vindicated.

Public-bank Q4 2026 EUR/USD range: 1.12–1.15 across the contemporaneously identifiable MUFG, ING and Commerzbank forecasts. This is a limited public-bank sample, not a formal forecast-distribution range.

Constructive USD cluster: EUR/USD 1.12–1.13 for Q4 2026, represented by MUFG and ING; ING also described a near-term trading environment concentrated in the lower half of 1.10–1.15.

More cautious / tactical USD view: EUR/USD approximately 1.15 at year-end or at the Reuters survey's 3–6 month horizon; the survey's 12-month median was 1.16. These are different forecast horizons and must not be treated as perfectly comparable targets.

Bias at window close: USD constructive versus EUR in the near term, but increasingly two-sided tactically; medium-term survey consensus still anticipates USD depreciation, and EUR/USD near 1.125 already discounts much of the USD-supportive Q4 bank forecast cluster.

What changed through the data window

Starting state — 4–5 October: dollar rally ahead of strategist forecasts.
The dollar entered the window following a September appreciation exceeding 3%, supported by the Fed's September tightening, elevated Treasury yields and global bond-market stress. Yet the Reuters survey retained a relatively stable weak-dollar forecast profile. The unusual configuration was not strong strategist conviction that the dollar should continue appreciating; it was a growing recognition that actual spot performance repeatedly exceeded bearish USD forecasts. The 2 October survey also documented persistent forecast errors: three-month strategist forecasts had underestimated dollar strength for nine consecutive months. This made the weak-dollar consensus vulnerable to continued US rate and growth outperformance.

8–13 October — European stress reinforces the USD relative-rate argument.
Dollar support increasingly combined US yield differentials with weakness in the euro itself. French fiscal and sovereign-bond concerns raised the euro's domestic risk premium, while elevated energy prices reinforced the inflation and terms-of-trade pressure on Europe. ING's 12 October strategic note identified an increasingly independent euro-weakness channel and adopted a lower EUR/USD range. Its 13 October commentary explicitly revised Q4/Q1 EUR/USD forecasts to 1.13. This constitutes a genuine forecast revision, not merely spot moving toward unchanged targets. The correction was important because an earlier dollar-bearish positioning framework increasingly required several conditions to improve together: US yields moderating, French fiscal risk stabilizing and the oil shock becoming less damaging to Europe. Sources: https://think.ing.com/bundles/fx-talking-au-revoir-euro-bulls/ ; https://think.ing.com/articles/fx-daily-no-trigger-in-sight-for-a-dollar-reversal/

14 October — CPI validates the tactical USD bull case, temporarily.
September US core CPI surprised to the upside, reinforcing the Fed-tightening narrative. DXY reached approximately 102.94 intraday and EUR/USD touched the 1.111 area. This was primarily spot convergence toward the USD-bullish tactical scenario, rather than evidence that the Reuters survey median had been formally revised. The market was pricing a stronger possibility of nearer-term Fed restriction while the euro remained vulnerable to European political and fiscal risk.

15–16 October — the hawkish inflation argument survives, but dollar price action reverses.
Despite strong producer and import-price inflation, US Treasury yields and the dollar retreated. Cautious Fed communication limited the willingness to price immediate tightening, while AI-related equity and credit concerns increased uncertainty over the durability of US financial-market outperformance. Reuters reported that by 16 October the dollar was heading toward its first weekly decline in more than a month against both the euro and yen. DXY stood near 101.87, down approximately 0.35% on the week, while EUR/USD had recovered toward 1.125. This is a meaningful tactical change: the same environment that had supported dollar appreciation through inflation and yield differentials began generating US financial-stability and growth concerns that could weigh on the currency. Sources: https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/euro-gets-much-needed-reprieve-ai-wobbles-rock-dollar-2026-10-16/ ; https://think.ing.com/articles/fx-daily-inflation-versus-ai-overbuild-story-dominates/
The window therefore closes with a more conditional USD bull case than the midweek inflation-price reaction alone suggested.

Main consensus drivers

Fed credibility / relative-rate differentials: The September Fed hike and subsequent inflation surprises supported higher US short-rate expectations and a stronger dollar. However, the public strategist survey continued to assume that eventual tightening would be less aggressive than market pricing, limiting medium-term USD conviction. The key distinction was between the level of US yields and further positive repricing surprises.

Oil / relative terms of trade: Elevated oil and fuel prices strengthened the US inflation and policy-rate channel while worsening Europe's energy-related vulnerabilities. The effect was not purely favorable for USD: persistent energy inflation could also damage US real consumption and risk assets, reducing the net benefit from higher nominal yields.

European sovereign and fiscal risk: French budget uncertainty and rising sovereign-risk premiums added a EUR-specific weakening channel. The move in EUR/USD was therefore not a pure expression of Fed expectations. A stabilization of European fiscal risk could support EUR/USD even without a meaningful dovish turn by the Fed.

US financial-market leadership / AI-risk transmission: Strong US investment and relative growth supported USD through capital-flow and earnings expectations. By 16 October, concerns about AI infrastructure financing, equity valuations and associated credit exposures complicated that framework. US-specific financial stress could undermine USD even while inflation remained elevated, especially if the resulting Treasury rally reflected reduced growth or tightening expectations.

Where consensus could be wrong

Consensus too bullish USD: The USD-supportive Q4 bank cluster may overestimate the persistence of US relative-rate advantage and underestimate the growth effects of the oil and financing shock. If retail-control weakness broadens into services consumption, real hiring remains subdued and financial-market stress lowers Treasury yields, EUR/USD could recover toward or above the 1.15 survey benchmark. A narrowing of French risk premiums would reinforce that move.

Consensus too cautious USD: The Reuters medium-term weak-dollar forecast may continue underestimating the persistence of US inflation, Fed restriction and dollar-supportive capital flows. If core-PCE inflation remains firm, US services demand stays resilient, European fiscal stress persists and US yields reprice higher without destabilizing financial markets, EUR/USD could retest the 1.11 area and remain nearer the USD-bullish 1.12–1.13 bank cluster than the survey's 1.15–1.16 medians.

Key falsification: The decisive combination is the relative movement of US core-PCE persistence, real consumption and hiring, Fed rate expectations, and French sovereign-risk premiums. A durable decline in US yields alongside stabilization in European risk would challenge the tactical USD bull case; sustained US inflation with resilient realized demand and continued European stress would challenge the medium-term weak-dollar consensus.

DATA WINDOW: 27 September 2026 to 3 October 2026

A. USD WEEK — MACRO SYNTHESIS

The US exited September with a firmer revised output/income baseline but a weaker labor transmission mechanism. Q2 real GDP was lifted to 2.2% annualized, private domestic final sales to 4.6% and real GDI to 2.6%; August real consumption rebounded 0.6%, manufacturing surveys remained expansionary and core capital-goods orders advanced 1.6%. Yet the incremental growth engine is uneven: AI/data-center and power-related investment dominates construction, conventional rate-sensitive building remains weak, factory shipments stalled and inventories/backlogs accumulated. Household consumption ran well ahead of flat real disposable income, lowering the saving rate to 4.1%, while Conference Board confidence collapsed to 81.9. The state transition is stronger measured final demand and capital-intensive activity without commensurate hiring or assured household-income durability.

Labor became the principal policy-patience signal: September payrolls rose only 29k versus 90k expected, earlier months were revised down a combined 60k, industry hiring diffusion weakened and earnings increased just 0.1% m/m. JOLTS vacancies and quits were subdued; claims of 197k and household employment +406k still argue against a firing cycle. Inflation is two-sided: core PCE at 0.2% m/m and 3.0% y/y partly reflects BEA remeasurement, while ISM Prices Paid surged to 77.9 amid energy, tariffs and supply pressure. The Fed's in-window communication clarified a separation between tightening destination and timing. Williams (29 September) saw no urgency and allowed one further increase late in 2026; Jefferson (1 October) emphasized the need for more evidence, reinforced by Bowman and post-payrolls Hammack on patience. Logan argued for at least 50bp more and Barr, Musalem and Kashkari retained a restrictive-destination concern, while higher long yields may supply part of the necessary restraint. The resulting regime is a conditional October-pause / later-hike bias, not an official meeting commitment: soft hiring and limited measured core diffusion slow the timetable, but persistent cost pass-through could revive it. USD short-rate support weakens at the October horizon without resolving longer-term policy or term-premium support.

B. USD MACRO SIGNAL SCOREBOARD

Growth: +
Supporting evidence:
Revised Q2 GDP +2.2% SAAR, private domestic final sales +4.6% and real GDI +2.6% materially strengthen the historical activity baseline. August real PCE +0.6%, ISM 54.5, S&P manufacturing PMI 55.9, core capital-goods orders +1.6% and private construction +1.1% confirm ongoing consumption/capex demand. Counterweights: flat factory shipments, ex-AI construction weakness, nominal price distortion, inventories +0.5% and consumer spending outrunning income. Improvement is positive but increasingly capital-intensive and uneven.

Labor: -
Supporting evidence:
September payroll +29k against +90k, -60k revisions, private payroll +46k, industry hiring diffusion 49.0 and hourly earnings +0.1% m/m signal deteriorating hiring and wage momentum. JOLTS openings 7.079m, private hires broadly flat and quits rate 1.9% confirm low mobility. Claims 197k initial / 1.701m continuing and household employment +406k prevent classification as a generalized firing shock.

Inflation: ~
Supporting evidence:
Core PCE +0.2% m/m, +3.0% y/y versus +0.3%/+3.3% polls and wages +0.1% support softer current underlying momentum, but annual BEA revisions explain a material portion of the y/y surprise; headline PCE remains 3.4% y/y. ISM Prices Paid 77.9 (71.1 prior), 16 of 18 industries reporting material-cost increases, and household 12-month inflation expectations 6.1% point to adverse pipeline risk. Consumer/core pass-through remains unproven.

Financial Conditions: -
Supporting evidence:
Long-dated Treasury yields remained elevated despite initial front-end rallies on PCE/payrolls; mortgages near 7%, imported energy/material inflation and tighter project financing restrain housing, conventional construction and real purchasing power. September's high yield volatility creates duration and sovereign-spread spillover risk. Logan explicitly acknowledged that higher term premiums may deliver some demand restraint, although she cautioned against model-dependent decomposition. Initial reductions in October-hike pricing provide only a partial offset; no combined data-release window is assigned a fictitious single-source market response.

Policy Constraint: ~
Supporting evidence:
Williams (29 Sep) explicitly said there was no urgency and one more hike might be appropriate late in 2026; Jefferson (1 Oct) required more data and independent FOMC judgment, while Bowman saw no urgent need and Hammack emphasized post-payrolls decision time. In contrast, Logan (1 Oct) estimated at least 50bp more tightening was required; Barr anticipated further adjustments, Musalem saw policy as somewhat accommodative and Kashkari expected additional 2026–27 hikes without prescribing October. September's 3.75–4.00% Fed target range and the prior SEP's additional-hike median anchor direction, not timing. Payroll/wage weakness and uncertain energy-to-core diffusion favor an October pause; resilient spending, low layoffs and upstream costs preserve later tightening risk. The committee's inferred tension is how restrictive policy needs to become versus how fast, partly conditioned by the rise in long yields; neither a hike nor a pause was formally committed.
