Institutional interpretation and evidence
The professional tape treated July housing prices as modestly firmer on an annual and seasonally adjusted basis, without declaring a housing-market recovery. 3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment
The decisive analytical distinction is that modest nominal appreciation has not restored real house-price growth or affordable turnover. The positive Reuters surprise is compatible with a cooling transaction market because seasonal adjustment, geographical dispersion and the lagged nature of the index materially qualify the current housing signal.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms
a. Adjusted versus unadjusted prices; metropolitan dispersion
The principal distinction is between annual nominal appreciation and weak contemporaneous unadjusted prices. The 20-city composite rose 0.32% seasonally adjusted but fell 0.01% unadjusted. The 10-city composite was +0.40% SA versus +0.03% NSA, and the national measure +0.29% SA versus +0.12% NSA. Seasonal adjustment therefore generates much of the favorable month-on-month appearance. Fourteen metros accelerated in annual appreciation, yet eleven recorded unadjusted monthly price declines and six of the nineteen reporting metros were below year-earlier levels. Detroit was unavailable due to continued Wayne County recording delays.

b. Real prices, mortgage transmission and shelter measurement
Geographical divergence was large: Chicago +6.9% y/y, New York +5.8%, Cleveland +4.2% versus Seattle -1.6%, Las Vegas -1.3% and Denver -1.1%. National prices +1.9% y/y remained below consumer inflation near 3.4%, implying a fourteenth consecutive real house-price decline. This is a real valuation adjustment without necessarily severe nominal price deflation. Higher mortgage rates can depress transactions, affordability and new construction well before they force existing-home prices significantly lower. House-price appreciation is also not a direct proxy for CPI shelter inflation; transmission differs in definition and timing.

c. Historical revisions and statistical-quality limitations
Data-quality caveats are meaningful: S&P's release contains inconsistent index levels between tables, Detroit's July estimate is missing, historical index data can be revised over two years and the adjusted/unadjusted monthly gap is unusually large. Hence the direction of modest nominal stabilization is more robust than a reading of +0.3% as strong current housing inflation.

C. State Transition & Historical Context
State transition: stabilization — nominal prices firm modestly, while weak unadjusted momentum, real declines and restrictive mortgage affordability prevent a broad housing-cycle upgrade.

Context from prior regional live file:
June had already shown firmer nominal Case-Shiller appreciation alongside weak transaction-sensitive housing conditions and regional dispersion. July extends nominal stabilization but continues the real-price adjustment. The housing cycle remains more constrained in affordability and turnover than in headline nominal prices.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: A secondary, lagged stabilization signal: stronger annual prices do not imply that restrictive mortgage conditions have stopped weighing on housing activity.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: Prices adjusted for seasonality look healthier than contemporaneous unadjusted values; regional losses and falling real valuations matter more than the headline for identifying future housing demand. This does not independently justify another Fed hike or a USD/front-end repricing; the FHFA release shared the same event window.

What to verify next: Subsequent unadjusted metro prices, mortgage rates near 7%, applications and transactions, starts, builder incentives and CPI shelter dynamics.

Macro configuration: Modest nominal stabilization + continued real valuation declines + regional divergence + restrictive housing finance.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment
The unusually large confidence miss has more significance because deterioration spans present conditions, hiring prospects and household expenditure intentions. It is neither mechanically recessionary nor cleanly disinflationary: labor uncertainty coexists with rising inflation fears, while the latest observed real consumption predates much of the survey deterioration.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms
a. Breadth of current-condition and labor-market deterioration
The breadth of the deterioration is the major signal. Present business conditions moved to a net -1.9 balance as 20.4% of respondents called conditions bad versus 18.5% good. Jobs-plentiful fell to 23.6% and jobs-hard-to-get rose to 21.9%, pushing the labor-market differential down 2.5 points to +1.7. Future jobs expectations were more negative still: 14.0% expected more jobs versus 28.4% expecting fewer. Future income expectations stayed net positive at +2.5, but weakened. This is consistent with a low-hire economy that feels difficult for potential job movers even while unemployment claims remain low.

b. Inflation expectations and purchase intentions
The inflation composition prevents a straightforward dovish reading. Average twelve-month household inflation expectations rose 0.3 point to 6.1% (median 5.1%); 68.4% expected higher interest rates. Write-ins increasingly referenced oil, gasoline and goods/services prices. Both home and vehicle purchase intentions weakened, and discretionary service plans softened, although domestic vacation intentions ticked up to 42.6%. The collapse spanned Democrats, Republicans and Independents, making a single-party explanation insufficient.

c. Survey timing versus realized spending and savings
Timing matters. Fieldwork ran 1–23 September and reflects the September Fed hike, energy pressures and job anxieties. August real PCE subsequently reported +0.6% m/m, but covers an earlier period. Strong realized spending funded partly through falling saving may coexist temporarily with depressed confidence. A durable demand conclusion requires September–October retail and real PCE confirmation; absent that, sentiment is a forward risk rather than observed expenditure contraction.

C. State Transition & Historical Context
State transition: deterioration — household anxiety spreads from expectations to current conditions and labor availability, with elevated inflation fear; realized consumption and low layoffs have not yet confirmed a demand break.

Context from prior regional live file:
August confidence had already been weak, especially in expectations. September's 81.9 brings a sharp deterioration in current business and labor perceptions, while realized spending remains comparatively resilient. The household regime becomes more vulnerable to energy and borrowing-cost pressure.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: The deterioration in jobs and current business perceptions deepens the consumer-fragility risk despite recently resilient measured expenditure.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: Soft job perceptions and purchase plans favor Fed patience if hard hiring and spending also weaken; rising inflation expectations argue against calling the survey a straightforward dovish surprise. The 10:00 EDT release coincided with JOLTS, so no independent yield or FX reaction is attributed. Softer growth expectations could reduce nominal yields even while inflation fears lift inflation-risk premia; an October pause and later hike are both conditional on incoming data.

What to verify next: Labor-market differential against unemployment and vacancies; real income, saving, retail spending, travel and durables, energy prices and financing costs.

Macro configuration: Weakening consumer sentiment + deteriorating job perceptions + high inflation expectations + still-resilient lagged consumption.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment
The substantial point-estimate decline reinforces weak hiring demand, but measurement precision limits a dramatic interpretation. The labor market is adjusting mainly through reduced openings, low mobility and restrained replacement hiring rather than a wave of dismissals, which explains coexistence with exceptionally low unemployment claims.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms
a. Revised openings level and sector uncertainty
The revised July level is essential: the Reuters prior of 7.271m was restated to 7.335m, making the August point-estimate drop larger. Openings rate fell to 4.3% from 4.4%; industries showing point-estimate declines included professional/business services (-119k), health care/social assistance (-115k), manufacturing (-54k) and construction (-48k). Retail, food services, finance and information improved. None of the individual industry changes established statistical significance, limiting strong sector-level claims.

b. Hiring, quits and labor-market mobility
Hires rose only 46k on the month; the improvement was government-led (+47k), while private hires were essentially unchanged at 4.846m. A flat quits rate of 1.9% signals diminished worker mobility and less job-switching wage pressure. Low layoffs indicate retention despite soft recruitment. The statistically significant fall in openings among very small establishments suggests financing or uncertainty pressure may be concentrated, but the underlying detailed magnitude was not sufficiently verified.

c. Cross-check against payrolls and claims; survey reliability
This is consistent with subsequent September payroll weakness and low weekly claims: firms suppress vacancies and replacement hiring before actively laying off workers. Low flow through the labor market limits workers' ability to change jobs, and can gradually weaken income and sentiment even with a still-low unemployment stock. JOLTS sampling uncertainty and low response rates favor interpretation of trends rather than precise monthly changes.

C. State Transition & Historical Context
State transition: continuation — labor-market mobility and recruitment remain subdued, with weaker vacancies but no confirmed transition toward broad job losses.

Context from prior regional live file:
Earlier JOLTS releases showed weak hiring and quits alongside relatively low layoffs. The August estimate extends that structure, while the upward July revision emphasizes measurement sensitivity. Cooling labor tightness continues predominantly through vacancies and churn rather than firing.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: Vacancies and quits provide a dovish labor-tightness signal, while job retention continues to limit recession-style easing urgency.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: The upward July vacancy revision makes the sequential decline larger; nevertheless statistically insignificant industry changes cannot support definitive sector claims. Flat private hires and low quits help explain subdued wage competition. No stand-alone JOLTS FX/rates reaction is identifiable because Consumer Confidence published concurrently. A sustained USD or front-end repricing would require corroborating payroll and inflation readings.

What to verify next: October vacancies and private hires, quits, layoffs, payroll breadth and unemployment-duration changes; confirmation from claims and wages.

Macro configuration: Fewer openings + weak churn and replacement hiring + muted wage pressure + continued low layoffs.

a. BEA annual update and the core-PCE measurement break
The large y/y core downside surprise should be decomposed into an annual-update effect and an August monthly signal. BEA revised income/outlays back to 2021, reworking three price categories: investment advice/portfolio management now uses industry employment and hours to extrapolate real services; legal services use a composite of five producer prices; software/accessories use a revised mix including game software and hosting/IT infrastructure. July annual core PCE was restated from 3.3% to 3.0%, and headline from 3.7% to 3.4%. The Q1 and Q2 core quarterly annualized measures were revised to 3.9% and 3.3%, respectively. Therefore the annual -0.3pp surprise is not a pure current-month inflation shock.

b. Current momentum, headline energy and the core disinflation test
The revised new series nonetheless shows calmer recent core momentum: August +0.2% after July +0.1%, three-month annualized core near 2.0%, six-month around 2.7% and annual 3.0%. It is appropriate to use this consistently remeasured history going forward. However, one +0.2% result does not establish completed convergence to 2%, and headline monthly inflation accelerated on energy: reported gasoline +4.4% and transportation service +1.4%. Headline y/y remains 3.4%.

c. Goods/services spending and the disposable-income financing gap
Consumption is unequivocally stronger in real terms: +$190.8bn nominal PCE, with goods +$114.1bn and services +$76.7bn. Real goods consumption increased around 1.3%, led by vehicles, furniture and recreation, while real services increased near 0.2%. This reverses July's revised +0.1% real PCE. But real DPI was 0.0% and nominal income +0.2%; the 4.1% saving rate therefore finances part of current demand. Annual revisions raised historic personal income and saving materially (2025 saving rate to 5.4%), indicating the household buffer had been underestimated, while the current marginal consumption-income gap remains real.

d. Wealth effects, demand sustainability and historical revisions
Consumption may be partly supported by gains in equity wealth concentrated among affluent households, unlike broad wage growth. With high energy bills and financing rates, continuation of +0.6% real spending is uncertain. A shift in market wealth or precautionary saving could produce retrenchment without immediate layoffs. Thus the correct profile is an improved measured underlying inflation path, robust present spending, and weaker marginal household funding quality.

C. State Transition & Historical Context
State transition: stabilization — the core inflation baseline and short-run momentum improve and real spending rebounds, but flat real income, lower saving and continuing energy pressure prevent a decisive disinflationary-growth regime change.

Context from prior regional live file:
July showed weak real consumption and core PCE previously reported at 3.3% y/y, amid headline inflation at 3.7%. The annual update revises the inflation baseline lower, while August reverses July's spending weakness. Household demand becomes firmer, but depends more on saving and asset wealth than contemporaneous real income.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: Lower revised core inflation permits a more patient Fed timetable, while strong real expenditure and elevated headline prices preserve conditional later tightening risk.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: The annual -0.3pp core surprise is not wholly new inflation relief; the new series also shows genuinely calmer recent monthly momentum. Household spending is supported by lower saving and potentially uneven asset-wealth gains, not matching real income growth. The observed initial USD and yields rally belongs to the combined BEA/GDP/trade window; it reversed according to the supplied market tape. A durable USD-bearish or Treasury-bullish assessment would require continuing benign core inflation, softer labor and slower real demand, rather than only shifting a hike from October to December.

What to verify next: September CPI/PPI and PCE, month-on-month core persistence, real income/spending mix, saving, wages and energy inflation.

Macro configuration: Softer remeasured core PCE + vigorous real consumption + flat real DPI + falling saving + continuing energy pressure.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment
The meaningful revision is not solely +0.7pp of headline GDP but the stronger private final-demand and income accounts beneath it. It raises confidence that earlier activity was resilient, while leaving the forward growth composition vulnerable to capital-investment concentration, wealth effects and the subsequent divergence between production and job creation.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms
a. Domestic final demand and GDP revision composition
The core activity signal is stronger domestic private final demand, not simply the +0.7pp headline GDP revision. Private final sales rose 4.6% SAAR after Q1 +1.8%; consumption grew 3.8% after Q1 +0.7%, and business investment excluding housing reportedly grew 9%. Nonresidential structures, revised construction data (including data centers), inventories, recreational goods, services and federal defense all contributed to the GDP revision. This establishes a broader source base than pure AI construction, although technology-linked capital expenditure is central to the forward risk. Strong equipment imports can simultaneously depress headline net exports and support domestic AI investment.

b. GDI, wage benchmarks and the historical national-accounts update
The income side corroborates stronger activity: Q2 real GDI was revised to 2.6% from 2.2%, GDP/GDI average to 2.4% from 1.8%. Q1 real GDI was raised from 1.2% to 2.5%, reducing the output/income discrepancy; new QCEW wage information contributed. The annual update raised 2024 and 2025 real GDP growth to 3.0% and 2.3%, respectively (+0.2pp each). These revisions imply the historical economy was firmer than first reported, but do not ensure future growth if labor income or wealth effects slow.

c. Sector output, profits, inflation and employment-intensity tension
Industry detail shows goods +2.3% and private services +2.5% real value added, while profits from current production increased $384bn (downward revision of $16.9bn). Core PCE quarterly inflation fell from Q1 3.9% to Q2 3.3%, but headline PCE increased from 4.2% to 5.0%, and the GDP deflator remained 6.1%. The upward real/reduced-core-price revision improves the measured growth/inflation mix but does not remove headline supply pressure. The subsequent September payroll +29k signals a divergence between capital-intensive production and employment creation; candidate explanations include productivity, concentration in high-margin/AI investment, or lagged weakening of demand. None is individually proven.

C. State Transition & Historical Context
State transition: continuation — first-half expansion is more resilient in revised output and income data, with strong domestic private demand and a softer revised core inflation path, but persistent headline prices and weak subsequent hiring remain constraints.

Context from prior regional live file:
The prior Q2 second estimate showed 1.5% headline GDP versus 4.2% private demand and 3.6% core PCE prices. The annual update raises GDP/GDI and private final demand while lowering the measured price path. Output resilience is more strongly supported, but Q3 hiring and final-price transmission remain uncertain.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: Revised output and income strength provide policy-restriction capacity, though new September labor and core-price data carry more immediate decision value.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: Consumption and business investment support the revised first-half growth mix, while AI-related capital spending may create concentration risk. Strong equipment imports can depress net exports and simultaneously sustain domestic investment. The core deflator revision improves measured supply/demand balance without removing headline pressure. Stronger final demand could support medium-term real yields and USD relative-growth performance. AI infrastructure adds sensitivity for equities and credit through project finance, imported hardware and wealth effects; no GDP-specific FX or rates move can be isolated from simultaneous BEA data.

What to verify next: Q3 real private final sales, GDI/GDP consistency, equipment and structures investment, corporate margins, payroll intensity and real consumer spending.

Macro configuration: Stronger revised domestic output/income + investment-led demand + softer core-price measures + weak subsequent hiring.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

This regional survey was fielded September 1–15, does not capture second-half month conditions, and is a weaker national activity proxy than ISM or the Census hard data. A large beat against consensus is therefore not by itself a signal of sustainable industrial acceleration.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment
The near-unchanged initial-claims count is less important than the sustained sub-200k level and falling continuing-claims stock. It distinguishes weak labor-market entry and churn from an actual firing cycle. Administrative definitions, reporting anomalies and small future revisions qualify exact weekly figures without changing the broader low-layoff inference.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms
a. Claims level, seasonal adjustment and insured-unemployment trend
Initial claims declined by 1k from the previous revised 198k; the near-zero movement carries less information than the sustained sub-200k level. Unadjusted claims were 156,738, down 7,979, compared with a smaller expected seasonal decrease. Continuing claims declined 11k to 1.701m, the lowest in the official 54-week table, and down materially versus 1.921m a year earlier. Unadjusted insured unemployment fell more than seasonal factors predicted. These readings favor resilient job retention, although administrative claims omit many unemployed workers and some categories of job separations.

b. Vintage/date discrepancies, revision and registration limits
Later official revisions changed the preliminary initial figure to 199k and continuing claims to 1.699m, without changing the low-firing inference. An advance Idaho zero in a state table was treated as a reporting anomaly rather than a macro event. JOLTS low quits/openings and weak payroll hiring are not inconsistent with low claims: businesses can freeze vacancy creation and retain incumbents at the same time. The report does not prove an accelerating re-employment rate, because the shrinking insured unemployment stock can reflect fewer new claimants rather than stronger job finding.

c. Low-hire/low-fire mechanism and labor-market flow implications
The central policy distinction is employment flows versus stocks. Weak payrolls and low job mobility reduce wage tightness; low layoffs and historically low insured unemployment limit an imminent recession signal. This can persist for some time before either recruitment recovers or household incomes and joblessness eventually weaken.

C. State Transition & Historical Context
State transition: continuation — exceptionally low new claims and declining insured unemployment preserve employment retention, while weak recruiting does not show a new labor-market acceleration.

Context from prior regional live file:
Claims had already been around 200k while payroll/job opening data suggested weak new hiring. This release extends the low-fire regime and shows no new insured-unemployment accumulation. Employment retention is robust but labor mobility remains poor.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: Exceptionally low layoffs give the Fed room to wait for inflation evidence rather than respond to a labor-break emergency.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: JOLTS vacancies, low quits and poor payroll breadth do not conflict with low claims: employers may retain incumbent staff while freezing recruitment. Declining continuing claims cannot by itself establish faster job-finding. The Reuters week labels must remain untouched despite official DOL date corrections; no distinct claims-window repricing was substantiated. Relative to a layoff-shock scenario, claims only modestly support rates and USD; real inflation remains the next policy constraint.

What to verify next: Four-week initial/continuing claims trends, job-finding duration, October payroll diffusion, quits and new layoffs.

Macro configuration: Very low firing + weak recruitment and mobility + resilient employment stock + unclear job-finding momentum.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment
The manufacturing headline indicates ongoing expansion with little sequential acceleration, whereas Prices Paid shows a much more powerful deterioration in the inflation pipeline. Broad reported supplier-cost inflation reflects both strong selected demand and supply shocks. Those cost increases should not be mechanically interpreted as final consumer inflation or Fed tightening necessity.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms
a. Orders, backlogs, production and limited hiring breadth
The major marginal signal is input inflation rather than the -0.1 monthly headline change. Manufacturing expanded for a ninth month and remained well above the 50 threshold. New Orders +1.6 points and Backlogs +4.6 strengthen the forward pipeline, while Production -1.6 implies slightly less current momentum. Employment +1.5 to 52.7 is directionally positive but only 15.3% reported adding workers against 14.5% cutting, so broad net hiring cannot be assumed. Manufacturing BLS +9k and weak employment diffusion support a selective, not sector-wide, hiring recovery.

b. Price diffusion across industry and cost categories
Prices Paid +6.8 to 77.9 is the central constraint. Sixteen of eighteen manufacturing industries saw increased costs, spanning steel, aluminum, copper, energy, freight, semiconductors and memory components. This is a diffusion measure indicating a large share of firms experiencing price rises, not a 77.9% price increase. The near-March-war price reading suggests that the materials shock has materially reaccelerated after stabilizing around 71 in previous months.

c. Demand-pull versus supply-push, inventories and negative company comments
Demand-pull and supply-push cannot be separated perfectly. AI infrastructure and reshoring/defense purchasing raise order books, while tariffs, geopolitical energy costs and material shortages independently raise delivered input prices. Customers' Inventories at 41.6 indicate perceived shortfalls that may sustain restocking; ISM Inventories at 48.6 and supplier deliveries at 59 suggest disruptions and limited stocks. However, respondent sentiment was notably negative: only 40% favorable comments; 46% of unfavorable comments referenced price volatility, 34% tariffs, 30% Iran war, 21% lead times. This is an environment where quantity expansion coexists with weak confidence and risk to margins.

d. Reconciliation with S&P and Census hard factory data
S&P PMI increased to 55.9 relative to August, while ISM headline was stable. Different survey panels, index weighting and safety-stock/delivery adjustments explain part of divergence. Both show manufacturing expansion and faster input costs. Unlike strong survey demand, hard shipments remain less convincing. Whether cost pressure becomes consumer inflation requires checking PPI, CPI, services inflation and margins, not directly converting ISM Prices Paid to a core inflation rate.

C. State Transition & Historical Context
State transition: deterioration in the manufacturing inflation mix — orders and activity remain resilient but upstream costs accelerate sharply; business confidence and real-demand breadth prevent a clean overheating call.

Context from prior regional live file:
August ISM showed manufacturing expansion at 54.6 with Prices Paid already elevated at 71.1, alongside tariffs and delivery delays. September preserves activity, strengthens orders and hiring at the margin and increases input prices sharply. The inflation risk worsens without an equally clear growth acceleration.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: Factory cost inflation raises the Fed price-stability constraint even as soft wages and payrolls weaken the case for immediate October tightening.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: AI, defense and reshoring demand support orders, while tariffs, energy and material shortages independently raise costs. An ISM Prices Paid index at 77.9 is a breadth indicator, not a 77.9% inflation rate. Limited output-price verification and weak real labor/demand breadth support keeping the pass-through question open. The post-10:00 yield rise cannot be separated perfectly from simultaneous Construction Spending. Higher policy expectations could support USD, but energy/terms-of-trade costs can damage household real income and manufacturing margins. The sector effect is asymmetric: selected AI/power suppliers benefit while energy-intensive and import-dependent businesses face costs.

What to verify next: September CPI and PPI, ISM Services Prices Paid, metals/fuel costs, core goods prices, factory output, margins and orders-to-shipments conversion.

Macro configuration: Resilient factory activity/orders + rapid upstream cost diffusion + supply bottlenecks + weak broad hiring and incomplete CPI pass-through.

UNITED STATES — Construction Spending (Aug)
Release Date: Thursday 1 October 2026 | Local Time: 16:00 (Europe/Paris)
Importance: ***

PM FLASH: August construction spending rose 0.9% m/m versus flat consensus; private construction gained 1.1%, led by data centers, while total spending remained 1.7% lower y/y.

PM READ-THROUGH: Private investment resilience is concentrated in AI/power infrastructure and renovations; financing-sensitive housing and traditional commercial projects remain weak, with nominal inflation distorting volumes.

PM DEBATE & KEY TAKEAWAYS: Debate: Does the headline reflect a meaningful construction rebound or unusually concentrated, statistically noisy growth? The total +0.9% gain is not distinguishable from zero at 90% confidence; private nonresidential gains are significant. Data-center spending dominates the marginal increase; deflate and verify breadth.

1. Reuters Data

RIC;Date;Time;Rel;Indicator;Period;Actual;Prior;Revised;Poll;Surprise
USTCNS=ECI;1 oct;16:00;Med;Construction Spending MM;Aug;0,9%;-0,5%;-0,1%;0,0%;0,90%

2. Professional Market Commentary

Institutional interpretation and evidence
Census reported construction spending +0.9% m/m against a flat poll, with July revised from -0.5% to -0.1%. Total activity was approximately $2.203tn SAAR; private spending increased a statistically significant 1.1%. The office category containing data centers increased 4.6% m/m and 29.8% y/y, while improvements to existing homes accounted for most residential gains. Nevertheless, total nominal spending remained 1.7% below a year earlier and 3.1% lower over January–August versus 2025.

Research, attribution and market context
KPMG Senior Economist Meagan Schoenberger emphasized prolonged ex-AI construction weakness, high borrowing costs, and large increases in nonlabor inputs. Associated Builders and Contractors Chief Economist Anirban Basu highlighted extraordinary data-center investment, but limited expected breadth outside data centers and power. AGC Chief Economist Ken Simonson warned of labor/material costs, rates and public-infrastructure funding risk. investingLive treated the headline as a growth beat but cautioned it was within the sampling margin of error. No construction-specific financial-market repricing was verified: ISM was published concurrently and the desk attributed long-yield moves to ISM Prices Paid.

Additional source context
Sources: https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/pdf/release.pdf ; https://kpmg.com/us/en/articles/2026/august-2026-construction-spending.html ; https://www.constructiondive.com/news/data-center-construction-spending-august/831954/

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment
August spending improves the recent nominal trajectory, but aggregate statistical uncertainty and high input-price inflation sharply qualify the apparent growth surprise. The reliable positive component is private nonresidential spending, overwhelmingly weighted toward data-center-related office projects. Residential strength mostly reflects renovations rather than a broad new-housing expansion.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms
a. Statistical significance and public/private composition
The Census 90% confidence interval for the +0.9% total change was ±1.0pp, including zero. In contrast, private construction +1.1% (±0.5pp) and private nonresidential +1.0% (±0.5pp) were statistically significant. Private residential +1.1% (±1.3pp) was not. Public spending +0.2% (±2.0pp) was also not significant. The point-estimate surprise therefore exceeds the statistical certainty of the total series.

b. Office/data-center spending and investment concentration
Private nonresidential annualized spending reached $773bn, with the office category accounting for an estimated $5.9bn of an $8bn monthly increase: roughly three quarters. Secondary industry estimates suggested data-center construction +7.5% m/m and +73% y/y to nearly $85bn annualized. These data-center figures are not separate lines in the opened official Census table. The National Accounts annual update reportedly raised previously estimated data-center construction materially, supporting a larger AI capex role in historical GDP.

c. Residential renovations versus new supply; conventional building weakness
Private residential spending reached $882bn SAAR but remained -4.8% y/y; single-family and multifamily new construction each increased only 0.2%, while improvements rose an estimated 2.5%. This suggests renovations rather than a new-homebuilding surge under mortgage rates near 7%. Office +29.8% y/y and power +9.7% contrast with manufacturing construction -19.8%, commercial -5.4%, lodging -10.1%. Spending rose in many nonresidential categories, but the marginal dollar contribution was narrow.

d. Nominal cost pressure and reliability of real-activity inference
All figures are nominal; KPMG cited nonlabor construction input costs +8.7% y/y, diesel +78%, and significant metals inflation. Hence stronger spending dollars do not automatically mean stronger physical construction volumes. Census warned total estimates can need multiple months for trend identification, with large first revisions. The regime is consequently investment-led resilience in specific project categories against continued ex-AI construction contraction.

C. State Transition & Historical Context
State transition: stabilization — statistically firmer private construction and data-center/power investment offset weak residential and traditional nonresidential categories, without establishing a broad real building recovery.

Context from prior regional live file:
July construction spending was initially reported down 0.5% as housing and conventional projects weakened. August's upward July revision and nominal rebound improve the short-term sequence, but the structure remains dominated by data centers while rate-sensitive building is weak.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: AI/power investment and private construction remain functional despite higher rates, but the conventional construction cycle is not broadly recovering.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: The marginal office/data-center contribution is large while manufacturing construction and new homebuilding remain weak. Price increases can raise nominal project spending without proportional physical construction, creating project-financing and return-on-investment risk. The Fed should not interpret the headline as proof of economy-wide overheating. Market reaction cannot be isolated from the simultaneous ISM report.

What to verify next: Next Census construction release, real/deflated spending, office and power project breadth, manufacturing construction, housing starts and mortgages, hyperscaler capex and infrastructure finance.

Macro configuration: AI-led private-building resilience + weak ex-AI construction + renovation-led housing + cost/financing constraints.

FRIDAY 2 OCTOBER 2026

UNITED STATES — Employment Situation: Payrolls / Unemployment / Earnings / Workweek (Sep)
Release Date: Friday 2 October 2026 | Local Time: 14:30 (Europe/Paris)
Importance: ****

PM FLASH: September payrolls rose just 29k versus 90k expected, with -60k back revisions; unemployment increased to 4.2% and earnings rose only 0.1% m/m.

PM READ-THROUGH: Hiring breadth and wage momentum deteriorated sharply, but low layoffs and a +406k household employment gain prevent identifying a broad firing cycle.

PM DEBATE & KEY TAKEAWAYS: Debate: Are low payroll gains below sustainable labor-force breakeven, or consistent with a near-zero-to-50k new normal? Key takeaways: Private hiring diffusion fell below 50; participation increased and new entrants lifted unemployment. Weak flows, not job destruction, drive the tension; future payroll vintages and claims decide.

2. Professional Market Commentary

Institutional interpretation and evidence
The September BLS Employment Situation was the week's decisive downside labor surprise. Total nonfarm payrolls rose +29k against +90k consensus, private payrolls +46k versus +85k, unemployment edged up to 4.2% from 4.1% and earnings rose only +0.1% m/m / +3.0% y/y, missing wage forecasts. July was revised from +21k to -10k and August from +162k to +133k, a combined -60k revision. BLS described payrolls and unemployment as little changed and the unemployment rate as within its 4.1–4.3% range since March.

Research, attribution and market context
Fitch's Olu Sonola, Vanguard's Adam Schickling and JPMorgan Wealth Management's Phil Camporeale emphasized a low-hire/low-fire labor regime and less wage-driven inflation; October hike urgency largely disappeared. Franklin Templeton's Jeff Schulze and Janus Henderson's Bradford Smith stressed Fed patience without declaring imminent labor breakdown. First Trust's Robert Stein and Brian Wesbury, and RBC Economics via the press, highlighted a far lower structural payroll breakeven, household employment strength and low layoffs, arguing that +29k may remain consistent with broadly stable unemployment. Economists' breakeven estimates ranged from near zero to about 50k monthly, making the level difficult to interpret in isolation. Capital Economics (Bradley Saunders) noted a possible influence from changes to Haitian work authorizations on health-care staffing, but BLS did not establish causation.

Additional source context
Immediate pre/post release desk levels showed 2-year UST 4.78% to 4.72%, 10-year 5.23% to 5.17%, USD/JPY 157.60 to 157.15, and October hike odds around 28% to 15%. Other sources quoted different probabilities/timestamps. The initial dovish front-end reaction is credible; reported later long-end reversal was not verified from directly opened closing data. The subsequent 10:00 EDT Factory Orders release is not assigned a separate reaction.

Additional source context
Sources: https://www.bls.gov/news.release/empsit.nr0.htm ; https://www.bls.gov/news.release/empsit.a.htm ; https://www.bls.gov/news.release/empsit.b.htm ; https://www.ftportfolios.com/Commentary/EconomicResearch/2026/10/2/nonfarm-payrolls-increased-29,000-in-september

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment
This is the largest incremental Fed-relevant downside release of the week because the headline miss is reinforced by revision losses, slowing wages and narrowing sector breadth. Yet rising participation and a stronger household employment estimate moderate a hard-landing inference. Weak labor absorption and a lower employment breakeven must be judged jointly rather than treating a +29k print as either full stability or a labor collapse.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms
a. Headline payrolls, revised months and three-month pace
The negative payroll surprise is reinforced by backward revisions and deteriorating hiring breadth. July is now -10k, August +133k and September +29k; the three-month total payroll average is around +51k and private payrolls around +54k. Net of revisions, the September print leaves aggregate payroll employment 31k lower than expected from the previous vintage. This materially weakens the August rebound interpretation without establishing cumulative employment collapse.

b. Sector contributions and white-collar versus goods-side divergence
Sector composition is mixed. Private +46k; government -17k. Construction +11k and manufacturing +9k provided a goods-sector offset. Health care +17k versus a +33k twelve-month average; private education/health broadly +20k. Leisure/hospitality +10k, retail +5.8k and transport/warehousing +7.6k contrasted with information -10k, finance -7k and professional/business services -9k (temporary-help -10.9k). The information/finance/business-service weakness suggests low labor demand beyond government staffing. Factory and construction jobs rose, consistent with capex resilience, but did not provide broad hiring.

c. Industry diffusion, wage income and aggregate workweek
Diffusion indexes sharpen the deterioration: private-industry hiring breadth 49.0 versus 57.6 in August; manufacturing 46.5 versus 63.9. Net sector additions can stay positive while more industries cut than add workers. Average hourly earnings +5 cents to $37.81, +0.1% m/m and +3.0% y/y; aggregate weekly hours unchanged, average workweek 34.4 hours. The aggregate weekly payroll index rose only +0.2% after +0.7%, supporting slowing labor-income flow despite stable hours.

d. Household survey, participation and joblessness composition
Household measures importantly moderate the bearish signal: labor force +485k, employment +406k, participation up to 61.8% from 61.6%, employment-population ratio up to 59.2%. Unemployment +78k was associated with new entrants/reentrants (+116k/+152k), while job losers fell 45k and job leavers fell 173k. Unrounded unemployment rose from roughly 4.141% to 4.175%; the rounded 4.2% partly reflects threshold crossing. Long-term unemployed roughly 1.94m (27.1% of jobless); involuntary part-time +111k to 4.50m, while U-6 reportedly eased to 7.6% (secondary source). This is labor supply entering faster than hiring absorbs it, not evidence of a firing wave.

e. Seasonal/breakeven uncertainty and competing labor scenarios
Late Labor Day may have amplified seasonal variation, and routine revisions remain material; neither seasonal concerns nor a low breakeven justifies ignoring falling breadth, weak wages and repeated payroll revisions. A lower breakeven can stabilize the jobless rate even in an economy with poor job mobility and weak income growth. Therefore distinguish a still-resilient employment stock from fragile hiring flows.

C. State Transition & Historical Context
State transition: deterioration — August's apparent hiring recovery reverses into a low-hire/low-fire regime with weak breadth and wage momentum, but no confirmed broad layoff cycle.

Context from prior regional live file:
July payroll weakness had appeared partly reversed by the initially strong August +162k. September's +29k and the revised negative July observation remove much of that recovery evidence. Household labor supply and low layoffs nonetheless protect the employment stock from a sudden-break interpretation.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: October Fed hike urgency falls materially as official recruitment and wages soften; no evidence establishes a near-term layoff-driven easing emergency.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: The low-hire/low-fire regime can persist with small positive payrolls when labor-force growth slows, but poor diffusion and softer aggregate earnings may eventually weaken consumption. Competing hypotheses are low-breakeven employment stability, AI/productivity-led output without hiring, and lagged income-driven consumption weakness; none is proven. An initial front-end rates rally and USD/JPY decline followed the release; a later long-end reversal was not verified. The USD downside may be limited if relative US growth remains firm and tightening is postponed rather than abandoned. December tightening remains conditional on subsequent CPI/core inflation and whether claims and real demand hold up.

What to verify next: Next payroll release and revisions, job diffusion, claims, quits, wage growth, total hours, participation and September CPI.

Macro configuration: Very weak payroll flow + low wage growth + deteriorating breadth + stronger household labor supply + no confirmed layoff wave.

UNITED STATES — Factory Orders / Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories and Orders (Aug)
Release Date: Friday 2 October 2026 | Local Time: 16:00 (Europe/Paris)
Importance: ***

PM FLASH: August factory orders rose 0.1%, in line with consensus; core capital-goods orders increased 1.6% but shipments rose only 0.5%, while inventories accumulated.

PM READ-THROUGH: The investment-order pipeline remains strong in selected equipment, yet completed factory activity and broad real manufacturing demand lag the nominal new-order signal.

PM DEBATE & KEY TAKEAWAYS: Professional insight: AI/power-related machinery demand supports capex, but commercial aircraft weakness suppresses the headline. Rising backlogs may reflect both orders and constrained supply; input/work-in-process inventories grow much faster than finished stocks. 2. Professional Market Commentary

Census M3 full report showed total new factory orders +0.1% m/m, matching consensus; July was revised from +0.9% to +0.8%. Nondefense capital-goods orders excluding aircraft advanced +1.6%, while associated shipments rose only +0.5%; total factory shipments were virtually unchanged after eight monthly increases. Unfilled orders increased +0.6% and inventories +0.5%. Research, attribution and market context
There was no independent current-release named bank economist debate and no factory-orders-specific market repricing. The prior 08:30 EDT payroll-market move cannot be reused as evidence for the 10:00 EDT M3 release.

Additional source context
Sources: https://www.census.gov/manufacturing/m3/prel/pdf/s-i-o.pdf ; https://wsau.com/2026/10/02/us-factory-orders-increase-slightly-in-august/ ; https://investinglive.com/news/us-factory-orders-for-the-month-of-august-0-1-versus-0-1-estimate/

3. Comment — Economist Layer

A. Economist Assessment
The unexceptional total-order headline masks a more constructive equipment-investment pipeline, but its economic value depends on fulfillment. Rising nominal orders and unfilled work coexist with stagnant aggregate shipments, expanding precautionary inventories and higher input prices. This is investment resilience, not a confirmed broad acceleration in physical output or delivered corporate revenue.

B. Detailed Evidence & Economic Mechanisms
a. Order composition, transport volatility and equipment categories
Total orders increased $0.7bn to $663.5bn; ex-transportation orders increased +0.3%, ex-defense +0.1%, durables -0.1%, nondurables +0.3%. Transportation -0.7% reflected commercial aircraft -4.3% after July +12%, partly offset by defense aircraft +5.9%. Machinery +1.1% included construction machinery +7.2%, mining/oil equipment +9.5% and turbines/generators +3.5%; industrial machinery -7.5%. Electrical equipment +1.1%; computers/electronics flat. This is a selective equipment capex pipeline, not broad uniform new-order growth.

b. Core equipment orders versus shipments and growing backlogs
Core nondefense capex orders +1.6% to $87.6bn, +10.6% year to date, are the strongest forward indicator. But core shipments +0.5% after July +1.4%, and total shipments unchanged at $658.6bn, show that purchasing commitments are outpacing fulfilled deliveries. Unfilled orders rose to $1.610tn (25 increases in 26 months) and the unfilled-orders/shipments ratio to 6.87 from 6.81. Bottlenecks can grow order books without the same increase in physical factory output.

c. Inventory location, precautionary purchasing and price distortion
Inventories increased to $972.4bn, an eleventh monthly gain, with materials/supplies +0.7%, work in process +0.9%, finished goods +0.1%, and inventory/shipments ratio 1.48 from 1.47. This looks more like supply insurance and delayed completion than a proven unwanted finished-goods stockpile, but creates future destocking risk if final demand slows. M3 is not price adjusted; elevated metal, energy and freight costs inflate nominal orders, backlogs and inventories. Semiconductor manufacturing is excluded from new/unfilled M3 orders, important when discussing AI. Census's nonprobability panel has no calculated confidence intervals, and seasonal adjustment/history updates were frozen for the remainder of 2026.

d. Survey-versus-hard-output reconciliation and measurement limits
Cross-check against surveys: S&P/ISM reported demand expansion and longer supplier delivery times, while shipment hard data barely moved. Hence the private-investment pipeline remains active but completed real output has not accelerated equivalently.

C. State Transition & Historical Context
State transition: stabilization — nominal orders and core equipment demand stay positive, but flat shipments, softer durables and rising inventory stocks prevent a broad manufacturing hard-output upgrade.

Context from prior regional live file:
July's factory orders rebound had been +0.9% before slight revision, with shipments and backlogs increasing. August maintains core equipment demand but slows realized shipments. Manufacturing resilience increasingly depends on converting the order book into production and revenue.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Main incremental information: Core equipment demand supports a resilient capex story without generating an independent Fed tightening signal from an in-line aggregate orders report.

Macro mechanism / strategic debate: Aircraft volatility and selected machinery strength conceal wide variation in factory demand. Supply bottlenecks may inflate backlog values while delaying deliveries; inventory increases in materials and work-in-process suggest insurance or unfinished production rather than proved unwanted finished goods. M3 excludes semiconductor new/unfilled orders and reports nominal values; no standalone rates/FX reaction is verified. For credit and equities, backlogs should be tested against fulfillment, working-capital demands, input costs and cash conversion; for USD/front-end rates this report remains secondary to payroll, PCE/CPI and ISM.

What to verify next: Subsequent deflated capital-goods orders and shipments, inventory composition, backlog fulfillment, industrial production, pricing and AI/equipment capex guidance.

Macro configuration: Strong selective equipment orders + flat factory shipments + rising backlogs/inventories + nominal-price and supply constraints.
D. CENTRAL BANK TAPE

Summary — Policy reaction function

The 16 September 2026 FOMC had raised the target range to 3.75–4.00% by a 12–0 vote; the September SEP (carry-over context, not a new window document) indicated a median 4.1% end-2026 funds-rate projection and broad support for at least one additional increase. Within 27 September–3 October, the pivotal change was in expected timing, not abandonment of inflation vigilance. Williams on 29 September and Jefferson on 1 October argued for time to assess inflation and financial transmission after September. Bowman echoed the absence of urgency; Kashkari was explicitly undecided about October; Hammack emphasized waiting for information after 2 October payrolls. Logan and other hawkish voices disputed the adequacy of the current policy level. The most defensible in-window interpretation is an October-pause bias with later tightening optionality, not Fed guidance that December is guaranteed. The Chair made no verified policy remarks in-window. Public interpretations from Evercore ISI, SGH's Tim Duy and Goldman Sachs read this as a meeting-timing reset; October pricing moved with both speakers and economic releases, so no isolated probability change is assigned.

No new FOMC statement or minutes were published during the window (minutes due 7 October and excluded). The scout's 7–8 October retrospective interpretations are excluded from this in-window policy conclusion.

Bottom line — central bank tape

The committee's center leaned toward more time between hikes, while directional tightening risk survived and terminal-rate conviction diverged: Williams' possible single late-year increase versus Logan's at-least-50bp requirement and Kashkari's 2027 extension. Payroll and wage weakness reinforced patience; low layoffs, robust investment demand and still-elevated input inflation prevented an easing inference. Watch realized core CPI/PCE and services diffusion, employment flows, and whether elevated term premiums deliver enough demand restraint to change the required funds-rate path. Do not treat an October pause or December hike as formally announced, nor use a single hawkish voter to infer the FOMC median.

E. SIGNAL TENSION CHECK

Main contradiction:
Capital-intensive US demand and manufacturing orders remain strong while labor hiring and wages soften; revised core PCE looks calmer even as input prices surge. Inside the Fed, Williams/Jefferson favor time to test this pass-through, while Logan/Musalem and Kashkari judge the ultimate policy level insufficiently restrictive, raising the question whether high long yields substitute for further front-end tightening.

Why it matters:
An October pause can coexist with additional later hikes, but neither output resilience nor the first-round supply-price shock establishes the correct terminal rate. Premature action could compound weak income and conventional investment; waiting too long risks persistent core inflation.

Implication:
Favor restrictive patience over a mechanical October hike, without treating December or the terminal rate as settled. Test consumer-price diffusion and inflation expectations against labor-income deceleration, hard shipments and the real activity restraint imposed by term premiums.

F. 5 KEY RELEASES TO DIG INTO

**** UNITED STATES — EMPLOYMENT SITUATION (2 OCT 2026)
Why it matters: Payrolls +29k versus +90k, private +46k, combined -60k backward revisions and weaker industry diffusion challenge the hiring-resilience case. Falling wages versus a strong household employment count and low claims isolate the key low-hire/low-fire ambiguity.

**** UNITED STATES — PERSONAL INCOME / CONSUMPTION / PCE INFLATION (30 SEP 2026)
Why it matters: Core PCE +0.2% m/m and 3.0% y/y improve the measured inflation path, but BEA remeasurement is critical. Real consumption +0.6% against zero real DPI and a 4.1% saving rate tests the sustainability of consumer strength.

**** UNITED STATES — ISM MANUFACTURING / PRICES PAID (1 OCT 2026)
Why it matters: ISM 54.5 and orders/backlogs expansion coexist with Prices Paid at 77.9, broad tariffs/energy/metals pressure and negative respondent color. PPI/CPI and output prices must establish whether pipeline pressure survives margin absorption.

**** UNITED STATES — CONFERENCE BOARD CONSUMER CONFIDENCE (29 SEP 2026)
Why it matters: Confidence 81.9 versus 89.2 poll, weaker labor perceptions and 6.1% inflation expectations place a leading-risk marker on real household demand even as August consumption was strong.

**** UNITED STATES — GDP THIRD ESTIMATE (30 SEP 2026)
Why it matters: Real GDP revised to 2.2%, private final demand to 4.6% and real GDI to 2.6% confirm an unusually firm historical baseline. Hard output, capital-expenditure breadth and future employment conversion must validate its persistence.

G. RED TEAM QUESTIONS

1. Can the September +29k payroll gain and weaker industry hiring breadth coexist durably with a low payroll breakeven, +406k household employment and low claims, or will the employment stock begin to deteriorate?

2. How much of core PCE's measured 3.3%-to-3.0% annual improvement is BEA remeasurement rather than true current disinflation, and will September CPI independently validate it?

3. Does ISM Prices Paid at 77.9 diffuse into persistent core services/goods prices and medium-term expectations, or remain an energy/tariff/AI supply-cost shock absorbed in margins and inventories?

4. Can August real PCE growth of +0.6% persist with flat real DPI, saving at 4.1%, confidence 81.9 and slowing wage/hiring flows, or will the consumer finally follow sentiment lower?

5. Will +1.6% core capital-goods orders become deflated shipments and broad employment gains, or does data-center construction concentration mask a narrower and more fragile real capex cycle?

6. What realized underlying-inflation or labor threshold would overturn the Williams–Jefferson/Bowman 'time to judge' interpretation and justify an October move rather than a later conditional hike?

7. Does Logan's +50bp-or-more destination imply a substantive committee split versus Williams' possible single late-2026 hike, or can higher Treasury term premiums deliver restriction that reconciles the paths without crushing housing and conventional investment?

H. CURRENCY MARKET-CONSENSUS SCAN

Bottom line

Primary comparison convention: EUR/USD (lower pair = stronger USD); DXY is the broad USD cross-check (higher = stronger USD). This is a historical 27 September–3 October 2026 consensus reconstruction, not an assessment of views prevailing after the window. At the window close, publicly visible FX strategists remained broadly bearish USD over six to twelve months, but were materially less confident that the dollar had finished its near-term rally. Reuters' poll of nearly 70 forecasters conducted 30 September–2 October put median EUR/USD at 1.14 in one month, 1.15 in three and six months and 1.16 in twelve months. Nearly 80% of near-term risk respondents nevertheless thought USD more likely to outperform than undershoot the three-month forecast. This is a split between forecast-level medium-term dollar depreciation and near-term USD upside skew, not a formal majority forecast for a sustained USD bull market.

The selected in-force public-bank end-Q4 EUR/USD targets ranged from 1.12 to 1.17: MUFG 1.12 (revised 1 October), BNP Paribas 1.14 (28 September), ING 1.16 (7 September still in force during the window) and Deutsche Bank 1.17 (30 September view relayed publicly). These are visible representative targets, NOT a formal bank-survey percentile range. The extreme USD-supportive revision came from MUFG: it cut its Q4 EUR/USD target from 1.18 to 1.12 during the window while still envisaging later dollar depreciation. ING's September revision from 1.18 to 1.16 was already in place before the start of this window. Thus aggregate forecasts remained more USD-bearish than spot, despite a fresh, identifiable in-window USD-bullish house revision.

EUR/USD finished 2 October near 1.1254 on a commonly reported end-of-day series, versus approximately 1.137 at the beginning of the week, while DXY closed near 101.93 on the same historical-data provider's index series. EUR/USD had already dropped below the Reuters 1.15 three/six-month median and below three of the four selected end-Q4 bank targets; it was only slightly above MUFG's 1.12. MUFG's dated 30 September spot convention placed DXY at 101.243 and its 1 October note forecast DXY 102.19 for end-Q4, which is a single-house index forecast, not a DXY consensus. The spot-to-target gap implied medium-term EUR recovery under the survey but poor immediate timing evidence: strong US yields and risk aversion were competing with the softer payrolls/PCE signal.

Public-bank Q4 2026 range: EUR/USD 1.12–1.17 (four selected in-force bank targets; lower = more bullish USD; not a survey distribution). A comparable multi-bank DXY forecast range was not established.

Constructive USD cluster: EUR/USD 1.12–1.14 end-Q4 (MUFG / BNP Paribas); MUFG DXY 102.19 end-Q4 is one bank's separately dated index target.

More cautious / tactical USD view: EUR/USD 1.16–1.17 end-Q4 (ING / Deutsche Bank); Reuters one-month median EUR/USD 1.14 and three/six-month median 1.15 are separately surveyed horizons, not end-Q4 bank targets.

Bias at window close: Tactical USD support with two-way event risk, but broader six-to-twelve-month strategist forecasts leaned USD depreciation. EUR/USD ~1.1254 was closer to the strong-USD bank tail than to Reuters' 1.15–1.16 recovery medians.

What changed through the data window

Entering the week, September's Fed hike, steep rise in US yields and risk aversion had already strengthened USD; ING's 7 September shift to a delayed dollar downtrend was the opening background, not a week-of revision. On 29–30 September, confidence/JOLTS weakness and a lower remeasured core PCE path reduced the case for immediate October tightening, but the higher long-yield and global bond-volatility channel continued supporting USD. On 1 October, ISM Prices Paid at 77.9 restored an inflation-risk argument even as construction spending confirmed heavy concentration in AI infrastructure. On 2 October, the weaker payroll/wage data caused an initial dollar/front-end rates decline, while reported long-duration selling remained a counterweight. Treat market reactions at simultaneous release windows as combined events rather than establishing isolated causality from one data print.

There were two distinct adjustments, not one: MUFG explicitly changed the forecast (end-Q4 EUR/USD 1.18 to 1.12); the wider Reuters sample made only minor revisions even as spot had moved materially toward the dollar-bullish end of existing public targets. Deutsche Bank's contemporaneous 1.17 year-end view and argument against chasing a USD breakout illustrate why near-term dollar momentum was not interchangeable with a unified medium-term bank consensus. The survey's nearly 80% upside-USD near-term risk balance was the clearest agreement on tactical asymmetry, not a reversal in the median forecast path. No post-3 October strategists' revisions or price action enter this historical scan.

Main consensus drivers

Fed path / relative rates: September tightening and higher front- and long-end Treasury yields restored carry and policy-differential support to USD; weak payrolls reduced immediate hike pricing, but energy/tariff inflation kept the later path two-sided. Longer-term USD-bearish forecasts depended on US policy eventually proving less restrictive than market-implied pricing.

US growth / global capital demand: Revised strong private final demand and AI capex supported US relative growth, equity investment and dollar asset demand. Narrow hiring, flat factory shipments and fragile consumption funding raised the risk that the capital-intensive engine would fail to become broad income growth.

Global bond volatility / risk premium: Higher US yields and risk-sensitive dollar demand favored near-term USD strength; yet yield gains caused by term premium, fiscal concerns or an impaired bond market need not translate into durable currency outperformance. Europe-specific energy and sovereign risk amplified EUR/USD downside asymmetry.

Positioning / valuation against targets: The dollar had already rallied substantially into the week and EUR/USD near 1.125 left little spot distance to MUFG's 1.12 defensive target but much greater distance to the Reuters 1.15–1.16 forecast medians. This increases the cost of chasing spot without confirming follow-through in relative short rates or risk sentiment.

Where consensus could be wrong

Consensus too bullish USD tactically: Payroll/hiring weakness becomes an income and consumption slowdown, September CPI fails to validate the factory cost shock, and front-end Fed repricing moves down while term-premium-driven long-yield gains fail to retain dollar support. EUR/USD could recover toward the 1.15–1.17 institutional cluster even without a dramatic new ECB hike cycle.

Consensus too cautious USD: Input inflation broadens into services/core consumer prices, real US investment and demand remain stronger than job data imply, the Fed maintains a higher terminal path and global bond/sovereign volatility sustains demand for dollars; EUR/USD could test or undershoot 1.12 even though aggregate forecasts expected recovery.

Key falsification: A sustained joint shift in US-versus-European front-end pricing, actual US core CPI/PCE and job/consumption momentum, confirmed against Treasury term premium and European sovereign spreads, determines whether DXY remains above its ~102 area and EUR/USD stays near 1.12 or rebounds toward the Reuters 1.15–1.16 medians.

A. USD WEEK — MACRO SYNTHESIS

Regime continuation: The U.S. entered 20–26 September with robust private activity, unusually low layoffs and an investment-led growth cushion, while rate-sensitive housing remained constrained and household confidence was weak. This was already a low-hire/low-fire, strong-growth configuration rather than the start of a new expansion. The 197k initial and 1.719mn continuing claims readings mainly extended the low-firing trend. New-home sales at 684k stabilized through builder incentives, falling effective prices and substantial inventory; the Q2 $246.0bn current-account deficit widened through goods imports but did not alter the near-term Fed/FX regime.

Genuine new evidence: September flash Composite PMI jumped to 58.4, with services at 58.7 and manufacturing at 57.0, shifting activity from services-led resilience toward simultaneous demand and hiring acceleration. Stronger backlogs and the fastest input-cost inflation since October 2022 worsened the growth/inflation mix, although selling-price pass-through remained incomplete. August core capital-goods orders surged 1.6% after an upward July revision, reversing the apparent forward-capex slowdown. Michigan's final 48.1 largely confirmed earlier household pessimism, while one-year inflation expectations at 4.6% and long-run expectations at 3.4% preserved the inflation-psychology risk. The in-window Fed tape separated pace from destination: Williams favored no October urgency and a possible late-year move, while Logan and Kashkari argued for additional tightening beyond the SEP median path. State transition: continuation and strengthening of domestic growth, with genuinely new capacity/cost tension and renewed capex momentum; policy timing leans toward October hold / December hike while terminal-rate risk remains skewed higher. Hard hiring, realized inflation pass-through and Waller's unresolved policy stance are the key tests.

B. USD MACRO SIGNAL SCOREBOARD
Growth: +
Supporting evidence:
Private-sector activity accelerated sharply and broadened across services and manufacturing, with Composite PMI at 58.4, strong domestic new orders and rising backlogs. Core capital-goods orders surged +1.6% after an upward July revision, new-home sales stabilized at 684k, and the wider goods deficit was consistent with strong domestic absorption rather than weak final demand.
Labor: +
Supporting evidence:
Initial claims remained exceptionally low at 197k, the four-week average fell toward 202k and continuing claims held near multi-year lows at 1.719mn. No firing cycle is visible. The qualification is that claims confirm job retention far more clearly than renewed gross hiring; the PMI hiring acceleration still requires payroll/JOLTS confirmation.
Inflation: -
Supporting evidence:
The September PMI showed aggregate input-cost inflation at its strongest since October 2022, with pressure spanning fuel, transport, raw materials and wages while capacity tightened. Michigan one-year inflation expectations jumped to 4.6% from 4.0% and long-run expectations edged to 3.4%, reversing the prior improvement. Selling-price pass-through remains incomplete, so realized persistence is not yet established.
Financial Conditions: -
Supporting evidence:
Rate-sensitive housing remains visibly constrained: builders are sustaining transactions through price cuts, mortgage-rate buydowns, incentives and cheaper product while inventory stays high and the construction pipeline remains weak. The tape therefore shows monetary restraint still operating even though it has not produced an aggregate demand break.
Policy Constraint: -
Supporting evidence:
The macro tape already gives the Fed strong growth cover and little labor-side reason to ease; the central-bank tape makes that constraint explicit. Williams favors slower cadence rather than stopping the cycle, while Logan and Kashkari push the terminal path beyond the SEP median and no captured voter argues that September should be the last hike. The immediate baseline shifts toward October hold / December hike, but the risk is a higher terminal rather than an earlier meeting move.
