### UNITED STATES — S&P Global Services / Composite PMI Final (Jul)

Release Date: 5 Aug 2026 | Local Time: 15:45
Importance: ***

1. Reuters Data

S&P Global Comp PMI Final: 54,5 | Prior: 53,6
S&P Global Svcs PMI Final: 54,6 | Prior: 53,6

2. Professional Market Commentary

S&P delivered a **strong demand-side counterweight to the weakening labor indicators**.

The Services PMI rose to 54.6 from 51.2 in June and above the 53.6 flash, while the Composite PMI reached 54.5 from 51.9. The July composite therefore signalled solid private-sector expansion and the strongest services momentum in several months. ([PMI S&P Global](https://www.pmi.spglobal.com/Public/Home/PressRelease/b7c4bbe33baf452bb7aeb58021ccfa14?utm_source=chatgpt.com "S&P Global US Services PMI"))

The producer’s own framing was nevertheless cautious on quality. The scout captured that stronger consumer-facing activity was partly linked to major event and holiday spending, while export demand remained weak and input costs accelerated on tariffs and energy.

S&P’s chief business economist interpreted the survey as consistent with faster growth at the start of Q3, but the World Cup / event-related boost means the July acceleration should not be extrapolated mechanically into August.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

The key message is **activity acceleration without equivalent labor-market acceleration**.

Signal hierarchy:

* services final: 54.6
* composite final: 54.5
* both materially above June finals
* new orders accelerated
* consumer-facing services were a major source of strength
* export demand remained weak
* input costs rose sharply
* part of the demand surge was explicitly event-related. ([PMI S&P Global](https://www.pmi.spglobal.com/Public/Home/PressRelease/b7c4bbe33baf452bb7aeb58021ccfa14?utm_source=chatgpt.com "S&P Global US Services PMI"))

This release is important because it prevents the labor slowdown from being read as an economy-wide demand collapse.

Services activity and orders were accelerating at the same time ADP and JOLTS showed weak hiring. That suggests firms were meeting stronger demand through productivity, existing labor capacity, hours, technology or cautious labor management rather than aggressive headcount expansion.

The configuration is therefore compatible with the broader productivity story: output can remain resilient even when employment growth slows sharply.

But the quality of July demand is uncertain. Event-related consumer spending can create a temporary services spike, and the deterioration in exports prevents a clean broad-based acceleration call.

The inflation side is also less favorable than the headline growth signal: rising input costs show services importing tariff/energy pressure even as labor-cost inflation begins to soften.

State transition: acceleration.

Context from prior regional live file:
The prior USD services sequence had remained significantly more resilient than manufacturing, but June surveys had suggested moderation and uneven employment conditions. July S&P reverses the activity slowdown sharply, with services and composite output accelerating to multi-month highs. However, the simultaneous hiring weakness and event-related demand boost mean the release strengthens the growth floor without proving a durable reacceleration in underlying services demand.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

This is the principal **growth-positive counterweight** to the deteriorating labor tape.

For the Fed, robust services activity argues against interpreting weak hiring as an imminent recession. But stronger activity accompanied by high input-cost pressure also preserves the supply-side inflation constraint.

The policy implication is therefore not “weak labor = ease.” It is “weak hiring reduces the need to tighten while activity remains strong enough to allow patience.”

For USD, the activity signal is supportive, partially offsetting ADP.

Primary verification test: ISM Services determines whether national services data confirm the S&P acceleration.

### UNITED STATES — ISM Services PMI (Jul)

Release Date: 5 Aug 2026 | Local Time: 16:00
Importance: ***

1. Reuters Data

ISM N-Mfg PMI: 54,1 | Prior: 54,0 | Reuters Poll: 54,5 | Surprise: -0,40

2. Professional Market Commentary

The headline was essentially stable, but the internal mix was considerably more important.

ISM Services registered 54.1, up only 0.1 point from June. Business Activity accelerated sharply to 59.1 and New Orders rose to 57.2, confirming firm demand. But Employment fell back into contraction at **47.4**, from 51.2, while Prices rose to **70.3** from 67.7. ([Institut de gestion des approvisionnements](https://www.ismworld.org/supply-management-news-and-reports/reports/ism-pmi-reports/services/july/ "June 2026 ISM® Services PMI® Report"))

This produces a distinctly mixed services configuration: **strong activity and new orders, contracting employment and renewed price pressure**.

ISM also reported slower supplier deliveries and continued supply challenges in selected technical labor and technology components. ([Institut de gestion des approvisionnements](https://www.ismworld.org/supply-management-news-and-reports/reports/ism-pmi-reports/services/july/ "June 2026 ISM® Services PMI® Report"))

3. Comment — Economist Layer

The unchanged headline conceals one of the most important internal divergences of the entire window.

Signal hierarchy:

* Services PMI: 54.1
* Business Activity: 59.1
* New Orders: 57.2
* Employment: 47.4
* Supplier Deliveries: 52.8
* Prices: 70.3
* Backlog of Orders: 50.9. ([Institut de gestion des approvisionnements](https://www.ismworld.org/supply-management-news-and-reports/reports/ism-pmi-reports/services/july/ "June 2026 ISM® Services PMI® Report"))

Activity itself is not weak. Business activity and new orders are running at levels consistent with strong services demand.

The labor signal is the opposite. Employment fell 3.8 points and returned to contraction after only one month above 50. ISM notes that employment has been below 50 in 12 of the past 18 months. ([Institut de gestion des approvisionnements](https://www.ismworld.org/supply-management-news-and-reports/reports/ism-pmi-reports/services/july/ "June 2026 ISM® Services PMI® Report"))

That is highly consistent with JOLTS and ADP. Firms are experiencing demand but are not translating it into comparable headcount growth.

This makes the hiring slowdown harder to explain as simply weak aggregate demand. Instead, three mechanisms may coexist:

* firms remain cautious about permanent recruitment
* productivity / technology allows output growth with less labor
* event-driven demand creates activity that businesses do not expect to persist.

The inflation mix is uncomfortable. Prices at 70.3 represent renewed input-cost pressure even as employment contracts. This is the clearest services-sector version of the week’s stagflationary tension: **strong nominal/survey demand, weak hiring, elevated costs**.

The S&P/ISM divergence is therefore much narrower than in manufacturing. S&P sees stronger overall services acceleration; ISM sees near-flat headline growth. But both show resilient activity, while ISM uniquely provides a much weaker employment signal.

State transition: deterioration in labor quality / continuation in activity.

Context from prior regional live file:
Services had remained the main stabilizing growth bucket in the USD archive, but employment internals were already weaker than activity. July preserves that split in unusually stark form: business activity and orders accelerate while employment contracts sharply and prices reaccelerate. The services regime therefore remains expansionary, but the labor intensity of that growth is falling and the cost environment remains restrictive.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

This is a **stagflationary internal mix**, but its Fed implication is still more hold-biased than hike-biased once the labor detail is included.

The hawkish interpretation is straightforward: activity and orders are strong while Prices returns above 70.

The dovish interpretation is equally important: employment at 47.4 confirms that weak hiring is no longer confined to isolated surveys.

The correct reaction-function map is therefore conditional:

* hot inflation + resilient demand could still reactivate the FOMC hawks
* but tightening into contracting services employment becomes increasingly difficult to justify without compelling inflation evidence.

For front-end rates, employment weakness should carry more policy weight than the tiny 0.4-point headline miss.

For USD, the release is mixed: strong demand supports growth while weak employment reduces rate support.

Primary verification test: NFP is now the decisive labor arbiter.

## THURSDAY 6 AUG 2026

### UNITED STATES — Productivity / Unit Labor Costs Preliminary (Q2)

Release Date: 6 Aug 2026 | Local Time: 14:30
Importance: ***

1. Reuters Data

Unit Labor Costs Prelim: 1,3% | Prior: 1,8% | Revised: 1,3% | Reuters Poll: 2,1% | Surprise: -0,80%
Productivity Prelim: 1,4% | Prior: 0,3% | Revised: 0,8% | Reuters Poll: 0,6% | Surprise: 0,80%

2. Professional Market Commentary

The professional tape treated the report as a materially better productivity / labor-cost combination than expected.

Nonfarm business productivity rose 1.4% annualized while unit labor costs increased only 1.3%. Q1 was revised in the same favorable direction.

Institutional commentary viewed modest ULC growth as meaningful inflation relief and raised the possibility—still tentative—that AI-related investment is beginning to appear in measured productivity.

A less benign counterpart was that workers were capturing unusually little of the resulting productivity gains.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

This is one of the cleanest cost-side disinflation signals in the USD sequence.

Signal hierarchy:

* productivity: +1.4% versus +0.6% poll
* Q1 productivity revised +0.3% → +0.8%
* ULC: +1.3% versus +2.1% poll
* Q1 ULC revised +1.8% → +1.3%
* output: +1.7%
* hours: +0.3%
* hourly compensation: +2.7%
* four-quarter ULC: +1.4%.

The important point is compensation-productivity arithmetic.

ECI showed compensation remaining sticky; the productivity report shows why that does not necessarily translate into comparable unit-cost pressure.

The favorable revisions strengthen the message.

This is supportive evidence for an improving productivity regime, but not proof that AI has already produced a structural economy-wide productivity break.

The household side is much less benign: real hourly compensation fell sharply and labor’s share of output fell to a series low, connecting directly to earlier low-saving and real-income concerns.

State transition: improvement.

Context from prior regional live file:
The prior productivity sequence had already shown unit labor costs moderating, but weak Q1 productivity had prevented a clean positive productivity interpretation. Q1 is now revised materially higher and Q2 extends the improvement, while unit labor costs remain subdued. The cost-side disinflation signal therefore strengthens materially, while the structural AI-productivity thesis moves from contradiction toward tentative confirmation rather than becoming established fact.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

This release materially weakens the immediate Fed-hike case.

The three July dissenters could point to sticky ECI, strong private demand and strong ISM. Productivity/ULC gives the majority a high-quality counterargument: compensation is not translating into accelerating cost per unit of output.

For front-end rates, this reduces the weight attached to ECI alone and increases the burden on payrolls/CPI to rebuild the hawkish case.

### UNITED STATES — Initial & Continuing Jobless Claims

Release Date: 6 Aug 2026 | Local Time: 14:30
Importance: ***

1. Reuters Data

Initial Jobless Clm: 199k | Prior: 198k | Reuters Poll: 202k | Surprise: -3,0k
Cont Jobless Clm: 1,801M | Prior: 1,777M | Reuters Poll: 1,790M | Surprise: 0,0110M

2. Professional Market Commentary

The release preserved the extraordinarily low-layoff picture while adding a counter-signal from continuing claims.

Initial claims remained below 200k while continuing claims rose.

The Reuters feed is fully reconciled with the official revision history; the earlier continuing-claims discrepancy was entirely a vintage issue.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

The labor market is increasingly well described as low-fire / low-churn rather than simply strong.

Signal hierarchy:

* initial claims: 199k
* third consecutive sub-200k observation
* four-week initial average below 200k
* continuing claims: 1.801M
* insured-unemployment rate unchanged.

The firing signal is unambiguously strong.

But continuing claims introduce the qualification that matters before payrolls: the stock of benefit recipients increased even though very few new workers were entering unemployment insurance.

This reconciles:

* initial claims → firms retain incumbent workers
* Conference Board → households perceive jobs as less plentiful
* JOLTS → hiring and quits frozen
* ADP → private hiring weak
* ISM Services → employment contracting
* continuing claims → displaced workers taking marginally longer to find work.

State transition: continuation.

Context from prior regional live file:
The USD archive had already established an unusually low-firing regime while repeatedly warning that claims said much less about recruitment. The latest 199k initial reading preserves that regime, but the rise in continuing claims modestly strengthens the low-hiring / frozen-churn interpretation. Labor retention remains exceptional; labor-market dynamism does not.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

This is still not a labor-easing trigger for the Fed.

But after JOLTS, ADP and ISM Services employment, low initial claims can no longer be used as sufficient evidence of broad labor strength.

The July payroll report becomes the decisive falsification test.

### UNITED STATES — Wholesale Inventories Revised (Jun)

Release Date: 6 Aug 2026 | Local Time: 16:00
Importance: **

1. Reuters Data

Wholesale Invt(y), R MM: 0,2% | Prior: 0,3% | Reuters Poll: 0,3% | Surprise: -0,10%

2. Professional Market Commentary

The final report revised June wholesale inventory growth down to 0.2%.

Sales remained much stronger than inventories on a year-on-year basis, leaving the inventories-to-sales ratio unusually low.

The broader configuration is therefore lean inventories rather than aggressive accumulation.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

This remains a lean-inventory configuration with latent restocking optionality, not evidence that restocking has already begun aggressively.

Signal hierarchy:

* inventories: +0.2% m/m
* inventories: +4.2% y/y
* sales: -3.0% m/m
* sales: +14.1% y/y
* inventory/sales ratio materially below the year-earlier level.

The y/y mismatch is more informative than the monthly move: sales are growing much faster than inventories.

This provides a plausible mechanism behind ISM Manufacturing’s unusually low customer-inventory reading.

But S&P Manufacturing provides the opposite near-term warning: some firms are explicitly running down precautionary stocks accumulated earlier in the year.

Hence two inventory processes can coexist:

* defensive excess stocks are being consumed
* underlying stocks relative to sales remain low enough to require later replenishment.

State transition: continuation.

Context from prior regional live file:
April and May had already shown sales rising substantially faster than wholesale inventories, driving the inventory-to-sales ratio sharply lower. June extends that pattern. Inventories remain lean enough to support future replenishment, but the transition from drawdown to a durable rebuilding cycle has not yet occurred.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

Secondary Fed relevance, but useful for growth composition.

A genuine Q3 restocking cycle would reinforce ISM’s strong production signal. Continued restraint would support S&P’s post-front-loading slowdown interpretation.

## FRIDAY 7 AUG 2026

### UNITED STATES — Employment Situation / Nonfarm Payrolls (Jul)

Release Date: 7 Aug 2026 | Local Time: 14:30
Importance: ****

1. Reuters Data

Non-Farm Payrolls: -23k | Prior: 57k | Revised: 20k | Reuters Poll: 80k | Surprise: -103,0k
Private Payrolls: 30k | Prior: 49k | Revised: 30k | Reuters Poll: 78k | Surprise: -48,0k
Unemployment Rate: 4,1% | Prior: 4,2% | Reuters Poll: 4,2% | Surprise: -0,10%
Average Earnings MM: 0,1% | Prior: 0,3% | Reuters Poll: 0,3% | Surprise: -0,20%
Average Earnings YY: 3,2% | Prior: 3,5% | Revised: 3,4% | Reuters Poll: 3,5% | Surprise: -0,30%
Average Workweek Hrs: 34,3 | Prior: 34,3 | Reuters Poll: 34,3 | Surprise: 0,00

2. Professional Market Commentary

The professional tape treated the report as a material hiring-side deterioration despite the fall in the unemployment rate.

Payrolls declined 23k versus an 80k Reuters consensus after June was revised down to only +20k. May was also revised heavily lower, leaving May and June together 103k weaker than previously estimated.

The weakness was not completely uniform. Local-government education accounted for a large portion of the July decline and may contain a seasonal component, while health care and construction still added jobs.

But institutional interpretation nonetheless shifted clearly toward a September hold because the negative print followed large backward revisions and left very little employment-growth cushion.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

This is the release that validates the low-hiring / low-firing regime building throughout the fortnight.

Signal hierarchy:

* payrolls: -23k versus +80k expected
* June revised +57k → +20k
* May revised +129k → +63k
* cumulative May–June revision: -103k
* private payrolls: +30k
* 12-month average payroll growth: +34k
* unemployment: falls to 4.1%
* participation: 61.4%
* participation down 0.7pp since January
* long-term unemployed: 1.8M
* temporary layoffs rose
* AHE: +0.1% m/m
* AHE: +3.2% y/y
* workweek unchanged.

The falling unemployment rate is not a clean positive labor signal. Labor-force participation is weak, making the decline in unemployment less reassuring.

The payroll weakness also cannot be dismissed as a single-month anomaly because the 103k downward revision changes the preceding trajectory.

The firing and hiring signals are now clearly divergent:

* initial claims remain historically low
* firms are not conducting broad layoffs
* JOLTS hiring and quits are frozen
* ADP private job creation slowed to 44k
* ISM Services employment contracted sharply
* continuing claims drifted higher
* private NFP rose only 30k
* the establishment survey now confirms very weak net employment creation.

The correct labor-state description is **frozen churn**, not “strong labor market” in the conventional expansionary sense.

Wage detail reinforces the message: AHE slowed to 0.1% m/m and 3.2% y/y while the workweek remained flat. Combined with strong productivity / low ULC, the labor-cost complex is materially less threatening for underlying inflation than ECI alone suggested.

There is nevertheless a counter-signal: local-government education accounted for a significant share of the negative headline and could partially reverse.

But even excluding that distortion, private payrolls were only +30k and earlier months were revised heavily downward.

State transition: deterioration.

Context from prior regional live file:
The prior USD sequence already showed unusually low firing alongside weak recruitment: claims were near historical lows, but the archive repeatedly warned that retention was stronger than hiring and that falling participation could keep unemployment deceptively contained. July payrolls supply the missing hard-data confirmation, with outright negative headline employment, only +30k private hiring and large backward revisions despite unemployment falling to 4.1%. Labor therefore moves from a low-hiring warning regime into a confirmed hiring stall, while the absence of a layoff cycle prevents a broader employment-collapse call.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

This release materially changes the Fed reaction-function distribution.

Before payrolls, the hawkish case rested on resilient private demand, exceptionally low claims, sticky ECI, strong manufacturing activity, strong services activity and three explicit July FOMC hike dissents.

Against that stood softer core PCE, weak JOLTS/ADP/ISM-services hiring internals and benign productivity / unit-labor-cost arithmetic.

NFP adds the decisive flagship labor-side argument to the majority’s case for patience.

The policy hierarchy becomes:

1. September hike is no longer the natural base case.
2. The three hawkish dissenters retain a valid inflation argument, especially if July CPI is hot.
3. They now need inflation evidence strong enough to justify tightening into a clearly deteriorating hiring environment.
4. The low unemployment rate is less reassuring because labor supply is contracting alongside weak job creation.
5. Core PCE + productivity/ULC + JOLTS quits + wages + NFP form a coherent counterweight to energy/tariff inflation.
6. Strong services and manufacturing activity prevent the labor slowdown from becoming a recession call.

For front-end rates, the distribution shifts decisively toward **hold-first**.

For USD, this is the major release in the fortnight that materially damages relative-policy support.

For risk assets, the initial “bad news is good news” interpretation remains valid only while labor deterioration is mild enough to produce policy relief without becoming a broader demand contraction.

Primary falsification tests:

* July CPI
* August payrolls
* participation
* claims
* whether the July local-education distortion reverses
* whether the low quits/hiring regime persists.

D. CENTRAL BANK TAPE

Summary — Policy reaction function

The Fed tape sharpens rather than overturns the macro-derived policy read. The 9–3 July hold formally established a three-member hike bloc, while Warsh’s presser preserved a deliberately low-guidance regime and normalized disagreement. Subsequent sourced reporting materially narrows the apparent gap between the Chair and the dissenters: Warsh is not a committed holder, but a **conditional hiker whose September trigger requires both hot inflation readings and market ratification through higher hike pricing**. The July payroll shock then weakened the labor premise behind the hawks and simultaneously pushed market pricing away from September, suppressing one of the Chair’s own trigger conditions. The resulting reaction function is **hold-first under stress, with tightening delayed rather than eliminated and July CPI/Jackson Hole becoming the next decisive arbitration points.**

FOMC decision — 29 Jul 2026
Importance: ****

Key policy signal:
The Committee held the target range at 3.50–3.75% on a 9–3 vote, with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan all dissenting in favor of an immediate 25bp hike. The unified dissent formally moved tightening from an external tail risk into an explicit Committee branch.

Representative quote:
“Activity remained solid.”

Incremental reaction function:
The vote establishes a committed hawkish bloc but not a hawkish majority. September entered the window as genuinely live because only a small number of majority voters would have needed to migrate toward the dissenters. The later labor deterioration materially raises that conversion bar: the hawks now need inflation persistence strong enough to justify tightening despite a confirmed hiring stall.

Warsh — FOMC press conference — 29 Jul 2026
Importance: ****

Key policy signal:
Warsh described the hold as “especially prudent at these uncertain times,” welcomed the three-way dissent as a “good family fight,” withheld conventional forward guidance and emphasized that the Fed would observe market reactions directly rather than pre-commit to a path.

Representative quote:
“Where necessary and appropriate, we will not hesitate to act.”

Incremental reaction function:
The Chair preserved optionality in both directions while deliberately shifting part of the information burden onto market prices. That makes financial conditions more endogenous to policy than under a conventional guidance regime: long-end yields can tighten conditions without an immediate funds-rate move, while front-end pricing can influence the perceived readiness of the Committee itself.

Warsh camp / FT sourced reporting — approximately 5–6 Aug 2026
Importance: ****

Key policy signal:
People close to Warsh indicated that he would be prepared to hike in September if incoming inflation readings were hot **and** markets ratcheted up expectations of tightening. The same reporting said Warsh recognized shortcomings in the initial communication regime, reaffirmed rates as the primary near-term instrument and deferred the broader institutional-reform agenda.

Representative quote:
No on-record Warsh quote was supplied for this item; the signal is sourced reporting rather than an attributable public statement.

Incremental reaction function:
This is the most important incremental policy information in the tape. Warsh moves from “undisclosed hold” to **two-sided / hike-capable**, and his trigger appears explicitly two-key: inflation evidence plus market validation. That makes the reaction function reflexive. After payrolls pushed September hike pricing sharply lower, the second key became harder to satisfy even before the next inflation print. A sufficiently hot CPI could reactivate both conditions simultaneously.

Jefferson — Stanford remarks, carry-over correction — 16 Jul 2026
Importance: ***

Key policy signal:
Jefferson’s earlier “sufficiently restrictive” framing was explicitly conditional rather than dovish: if inflation failed to cool, he was prepared to reconsider the policy stance.

Representative quote:
“If inflation does not start to cool down soon... it could be appropriate to reconsider our current policy stance.”

Incremental reaction function:
The Board center is better characterized as conditional-hold than committed-hold. Together with Waller’s hike-permissive stance and Warsh’s sourced two-key trigger, this means the 9-vote majority is softer than the raw vote count implies. The payroll deterioration keeps that center anchored for now, but another hot inflation sequence could erode the majority quickly.

Bottom line — central bank tape

The central-bank overlay confirms **hawkish optionality but changes its timing and activation conditions**. The dissenters are institutionally committed, and the Chair is closer to them than the 9–3 vote initially suggested, but the post-meeting data have removed the clean labor justification for an immediate move and market pricing has moved against Warsh’s own second trigger. September therefore shifts from live-hike base risk to **hold-first conditionality**. July CPI must now do double work—re-establish underlying inflation persistence and re-arm market pricing—to make September tightening central again. Jackson Hole becomes the communication reset through which Warsh must reconcile the no-guidance doctrine, the labor deterioration and the still-live inflation threat.

E. SIGNAL TENSION CHECK

Main contradiction: Private demand, AI-heavy capex and survey activity remain resilient, while the labor market has shifted into a confirmed low-hiring regime and underlying labor-cost inflation has softened.

Why it matters: The Fed no longer faces above-target inflation against an unambiguously strong labor market. It faces supply/tariff/energy inflation risk against weak hiring but still-low layoffs, while actual activity remains too resilient for a recession-policy response.

Implication: **Hold-first is now the dominant near-term reaction-function configuration. Tightening remains conditional on renewed underlying inflation persistence rather than activity strength alone; easing requires the hiring stall to broaden into clearer demand or layoff weakness.**

F. 5 KEY RELEASES TO DIG INTO

**** Employment Situation / Nonfarm Payrolls (7 Aug 2026)

Why it matters: The decisive labor-regime release. Payrolls fell 23k versus +80k expected, May–June were revised down by a cumulative 103k, private payrolls rose only 30k and wage growth slowed. It validates the low-hire / low-fire regime and materially raises the inflation burden required to justify a September hike.

**** FOMC Rate Decision (29 Jul 2026)

Why it matters: The 9–3 hold formally established a three-member hike bloc while Warsh preserved a low-guidance, tightening-permissive framework. It moved the policy debate from whether a hike branch existed to what data would activate it.

**** Personal Income / Consumption / PCE Price Index (30 Jul 2026)

Why it matters: Core PCE slowed to 0.1% m/m while real consumption remained 0.4%, giving the Fed high-quality underlying disinflation without an activity collapse. The 2.7% saving rate simultaneously increases the economy’s vulnerability to a later labor or income shock.

**** GDP Advance / Core PCE Prices Advance (Q2) (30 Jul 2026)

Why it matters: The 1.5% headline GDP miss concealed 3.9% real final sales to private domestic purchasers, 3.2% consumption and 15.2% equipment investment. It is the clearest hard-data evidence that resilient private demand and AI-heavy capex coexist with softer headline growth.

*** Productivity / Unit Labor Costs Preliminary (Q2) (6 Aug 2026)

Why it matters: Productivity rose 1.4% while ULC increased only 1.3%, both materially better than expected with favorable prior revisions. The release weakens the wage-cost case for tightening and provides the cleanest supply-side counterweight to sticky ECI and elevated survey prices.

G. RED TEAM QUESTIONS

1. Does July payroll weakness persist once the local-government education distortion reverses, or do August payrolls and participation confirm that the hiring stall is broader and structural?

2. Can a hot July CPI rebuild both legs of Warsh’s reported September trigger—underlying inflation persistence and higher market hike pricing—despite weaker payrolls, wages and unit labor costs?

3. Is the productivity / low-ULC improvement broad enough to represent a genuine supply-side regime shift, or is it concentrated in AI-heavy sectors and vulnerable to revision?

4. Does resilient private domestic demand remain strong once the 2.7% saving rate, weak hiring and softer income growth begin to constrain household spending?

5. Which manufacturing signal is leading: ISM’s broad 55.6 acceleration or S&P’s slower orders/output and inventory unwind? What do hard production and shipment data need to show to resolve the divergence?

6. Do low initial claims continue to prevent a labor-break interpretation if continuing claims, hiring, quits and payroll growth remain weak?

7. Are tariff, energy and supply-chain price pressures strong enough to reaccelerate core inflation, or will productivity, softer wages and weaker labor mobility absorb enough of the shock to keep underlying inflation on a downward path?

H. CURRENCY MARKET-CONSENSUS SCAN

### Bottom line

Pair convention: EUR/USD, where a lower pair is a stronger USD.

The window began with the public FX consensus still leaning toward eventual dollar weakness. The Reuters 26 June–1 July strategist poll had EUR/USD at 1.16 by end-Q3, 1.17 at year-end and 1.18 in twelve months, even though a growing minority expected the dollar’s rebound to persist. That view remained contested by a stronger-USD camp led publicly by Bank of America, while Citi had identified EUR/USD 1.11 as a non-base-case downside scenario if inflation and Fed hawkishness surprised higher.

The 29 July FOMC did not initially validate the stronger-dollar view. The Fed held 3.50–3.75% despite three hike dissents, the dollar index fell to 101.07 and EUR/USD rose to 1.14315. But the more important consensus change occurred inside the second week. MUFG’s 3 August outlook cut its Q3 EUR/USD forecast to 1.14 from the prior 1.16 and argued that the dollar should remain supported for longer as Fed hike pricing persisted. Its displayed market consensus was 1.15 for Q3. The 31 July–5 August Reuters poll then confirmed the broader shift: strategists expected the dollar to stay firm in coming months, with EUR/USD around 1.15 over the next three months before rising to 1.16 by end-January and 1.18 in a year.

The 7 August payroll shock then challenged that freshly strengthened-dollar consensus almost immediately. EUR/USD rose to 1.1568, the dollar index fell to 99.50 and markets moved to a 56% probability of a September hold. The fortnight therefore contains a genuine forecast revision followed by a late data shock: institutional targets moved down toward 1.14–1.15 as the Fed remained hike-capable, but spot ended the window above that revised short-horizon cluster after the labor report undermined the tightening case.

**Public-bank / strategist Q3–3M range:** EUR/USD 1.14–1.15 for the central public forecast cluster visible during the window.

**Constructive USD cluster:** EUR/USD 1.14–1.15, with MUFG at 1.14 for Q3 and the 31 Jul–5 Aug Reuters survey around 1.15 over three months.

**More cautious / tactical view:** EUR/USD 1.16 by end-January 2027 and 1.18 at twelve months in the August Reuters poll; Citi’s earlier 1.11 level remained a hawkish-inflation downside tail rather than the central forecast.

**Bias at window close:** The market had just flipped back against USD tactically. EUR/USD at 1.1568 stood above the revised 1.14–1.15 Q3 / 3M cluster after payrolls pushed a September hike out of the base case, even though medium-term dollar depreciation remained gradual rather than aggressive.

### What changed through the data window

The first phase was FOMC uncertainty. Ahead of 29 July, markets treated the meeting as unusually live. The actual 9–3 hold produced an initially dollar-negative reaction: EUR/USD rose to 1.14315 as investors focused on the majority decision rather than extrapolating the dissents directly into an immediate hike.

The second phase was a material consensus revision toward stronger near-term USD. By 3 August, MUFG had lowered its Q3 EUR/USD forecast to 1.14 and explicitly shifted the expected timing of broader dollar depreciation into 2027. On 5 August, the Reuters FX poll described the dollar as likely to remain firm in coming months and put EUR/USD around 1.15 on a three-month horizon. This was not merely spot moving toward an unchanged target: the public forecast itself had moved lower from the 1.16 Q3 median published at the start of July.

The third phase was the payroll reversal. Ahead of NFP, EUR/USD was around 1.1521 on 6 August as markets waited for confirmation of the labor outlook. The -23k payroll print, large backward revisions and weaker wage growth then cut the September-hike case, lifting EUR/USD to 1.1568 and lowering the dollar index to 99.50 on 7 August. Spot therefore moved abruptly above the newly revised 1.14–1.15 short-horizon consensus cluster.

A separate flow distortion also affected the dollar complex during the window: coordinated U.S.-Japan yen intervention at the turn of August generated large moves in USD/JPY and complicated interpretation of DXY. EUR/USD therefore remains the cleaner core pair for the USD consensus reconstruction.

### Main consensus drivers

**Fed / rate differentials:**
The central driver shifted twice. Three July FOMC dissents and persistent hike optionality supported near-term USD forecasts, but the payroll shock reduced the probability that September would be the tightening venue.

**Relative U.S. growth / productivity:**
Strong private domestic demand, AI-heavy capex, services activity and improving productivity supported the view that the U.S. economy could tolerate restrictive policy better than peers. That growth premium prevented strategists from moving immediately back to an aggressive dollar-bearish stance.

**Labor / policy asymmetry:**
Low claims supported USD through labor resilience, but frozen JOLTS flows, weak ADP, contracting ISM Services employment and finally negative payrolls shifted the relevant labor signal from retention to hiring. That sharply weakened the marginal policy support for USD.

**Energy, tariffs and geopolitical / flow effects:**
Energy and tariff risks preserved a hawkish inflation tail, while Middle East stress supported safe-haven demand. At the same time, coordinated yen intervention created a large non-macro flow shock in the dollar complex, reducing the usefulness of DXY alone as a clean policy signal.

### Where consensus could be wrong

**Consensus too bullish USD:**
If weak hiring persists and benign core inflation / ULC continue, the September hike branch could remain closed and EUR/USD could stay above the revised 1.14–1.15 short-horizon cluster, accelerating the medium-term move toward 1.16–1.18.

**Consensus too cautious USD:**
If July CPI reaccelerates enough to rebuild market hike pricing while strong services, capex and low layoffs continue, Warsh’s conditional tightening trigger could reactivate and drive EUR/USD back toward 1.14 or below.

**Key falsification:**
Whether hot inflation can re-arm a September Fed hike after the payroll shock without the hiring stall broadening into layoffs, weaker consumption or a clearer demand slowdown.

Sources used for this historical scan: Reuters FX strategist poll, 1 Jul 2026; Reuters Fed/FX market report, 29 Jul 2026; MUFG Monthly Foreign Exchange Outlook, 3 Aug 2026; Reuters FX poll, 5 Aug 2026; Reuters FX market reports, 3 Aug, 6 Aug and 7 Aug 2026.

DATA WINDOW: 20 Jul 2026 to 24 Jul 2026

A. USD WEEK — MACRO SYNTHESIS

US activity strengthened but remained uneven: services delivered a sharp, partly event-supported acceleration, housing shifted from deterioration to tentative stabilization, and exceptionally low claims reinforced the absence of a firing cycle. The improvement did not amount to a broad demand or hiring boom, as manufacturing output weakened, housing remained dependent on affordability concessions, and the labor market continued to show stronger retention than recruitment.

The policy regime tightened more materially than the domestic releases alone implied. Renewed Iran and Hormuz disruption pushed oil above $100, while a new broad tariff wave introduced a second cost-push channel immediately before the July FOMC meeting. With the Committee fully under blackout, the resulting hawkish drift was expressed through market repricing rather than confirmed Fed communication. The final configuration was a resilient but narrow growth floor, persistent rate-sensitive weakness and a sharply less favorable inflation-risk distribution, consistent with a hawkish hold while leaving a material minority risk of an earlier hike.

B. USD MACRO SIGNAL SCOREBOARD

Growth: +
Supporting evidence:
The flash Composite PMI rose to an eight-month high as services accelerated sharply, while new-home sales exceeded consensus and May was revised materially higher. The improvement remained uneven: services received temporary support from major summer events, manufacturing output fell to a four-month low, and housing inventory stayed elevated at 9.3 months of supply.

Labor: +
Supporting evidence:
Initial claims fell to 187,000, the four-week average declined to 207,500, and continuing claims eased to 1.796 million. The data strongly reject an emerging firing cycle, but they provide limited evidence of a broad hiring acceleration, with summer seasonality and divergence between adjusted and unadjusted continuing claims qualifying the improvement.

Inflation: -
Supporting evidence:
PMI input costs and selling-price inflation accelerated as energy, freight, tariffs and renewed supply disruption raised business costs. The combination of faster services activity and stronger price pass-through produced a less favorable growth-inflation mix and increased the risk that supply-side pressure persists despite uneven underlying demand.

Financial Conditions: -
Supporting evidence:
Housing remained constrained by mortgage affordability, elevated inventories and a shift toward lower-priced transactions, showing that restrictive rates continue to transmit into the real economy. Simultaneously, higher energy, freight and supply-chain costs tightened business operating conditions even as headline activity improved.

Policy Constraint: -
Supporting evidence:
Exceptionally low layoffs and stronger services activity had already reduced the case for Federal Reserve insurance easing. The subsequent oil escalation and broad tariff action materially strengthened the inflation-risk branch immediately before the July meeting, while blackout conditions left the Committee’s response unconfirmed. A hold remained the consensus outcome, but the burden shifted toward hawkish communication and a higher probability of a September hike unless energy, tariff or inflation pressure reverses quickly.

THURSDAY 23 JUL 2026

UNITED STATES — Initial and Continuing Jobless Claims

Release Date: 23 Jul 2026 | Local Time: 14:30
Importance: ***

1. Reuters Data

Initial Jobless Claims: 187k | Prior: 208k | Revised: 209k | Reuters Poll: 212k | Surprise: -25,0k

Continuing Jobless Claims: 1,796M | Prior: 1,805M | Revised: 1,798M | Reuters Poll: 1,807M | Surprise: -0,0110M

2. Professional Market Commentary

The professional tape treated the release as a strong low-layoff signal, but not as evidence of a broad hiring acceleration.

Initial claims fell sharply to 187,000, an historically exceptional level, while continuing claims declined to a six-week low of 1.796 million. Reuters framed the labor market as remaining on an “even keel”: dismissals are very limited, but employment creation and labor-market turnover remain subdued.

Matthew Martin of Oxford Economics judged that summer seasonal noise may have contributed to the weekly fall but argued that the extremely low claims level and improving continuing-claims trend were difficult to ignore. Oliver Allen of Pantheon Macroeconomics also viewed layoff activity as subdued, with WARN notices and announced job cuts not pointing to an imminent dismissal cycle.

The main qualification was summer auto-industry seasonality. Temporary plant shutdowns and annual retooling schedules can make July claims particularly volatile, leaving scope for initial filings to rebound toward their recent low-200,000 range.

The policy tape was nevertheless hawkish at the margin. A labor market showing little evidence of a firing cycle leaves the Federal Reserve freer to focus on inflation and the renewed energy shock. Market tightening after the report could not be attributed to claims alone because oil prices and Middle East developments were material concurrent drivers.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

The release strengthens the job-retention side of the labor regime.

Signal hierarchy:

* initial claims fell 22,000 to 187,000
* the four-week initial-claims average declined to 207,500
* continuing claims fell modestly to 1.796 million
* the continuing-claims four-week average declined to 1.80525 million
* the insured-unemployment rate remained at 1.2%
* unadjusted initial filings fell more sharply than seasonal factors had anticipated
* unadjusted continuing claims rose while the seasonally adjusted measure declined
* summer seasonal volatility remains a material qualification
* the data say considerably more about firing than hiring

The initial-claims fall is not purely a seasonal-adjustment artifact. Unadjusted filings declined by 53,718, compared with the 31,379 decline embedded in the seasonal factors. The raw state-program data therefore also show a large reduction in new benefit applications.

However, the seasonally adjusted and unadjusted continuing-claims series moved in opposite directions. Seasonally adjusted insured unemployment fell by 2,000, while unadjusted insured unemployment rose by 13,891. This does not invalidate the release, but it argues against treating the weekly continuing-claims move as a decisive improvement in re-employment conditions.

The distinction between initial and continuing claims remains central:

* initial claims measure the incidence of new job separation and are a leading labor indicator
* continuing claims provide slower confirmation of whether displaced workers are being reabsorbed
* the very low initial reading is clear evidence against an emerging firing cycle
* the smaller continuing-claims improvement is encouraging but does not establish that hiring flows have strengthened materially

The report therefore improves the labor configuration without overturning the low-hiring side of the regime. Employers are retaining workers, but claims alone cannot determine whether firms have restarted recruitment, increased hours or broadened payroll growth.

The Reuters mechanical period fields appear misaligned with the official DOL reference weeks. The official report covers the week ending 18 July for initial claims and the week ending 11 July for continuing claims. Section 1 preserves the Reuters labels unchanged, while the official dates govern the analytical interpretation.

State transition: improvement.

Context from prior regional live file:

The prior claims sequence had already established a low-firing labor regime, with initial claims at 208,000 and continuing claims near 1.8 million, but it had not overturned weak hiring, payroll and participation evidence. The 187,000 print strengthens the low-firing signal, while the decline in continuing claims modestly improves the re-employment margin. Labor is more resilient than the weak-hiring narrative alone implies, but it has not yet transitioned into a broad hiring acceleration.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

The release reduces the probability that labor weakness becomes an immediate Federal Reserve easing trigger.

The reaction-function implication is conditionally hawkish:

* the firing channel is clearly subdued
* continuing claims are no longer moving higher at the margin
* marginal PMI employment growth provides some cross-survey confirmation
* the Fed can continue to prioritize inflation while labor retention remains strong
* the signal does not prove payroll acceleration or stronger labor demand
* seasonal normalization could reverse part of the initial-claims move quickly

For front-end rates, the print reinforces a hawkish asymmetry rather than creating a standalone tightening signal. A very low layoff rate reduces the urgency to insure against labor deterioration, but the magnitude of market repricing cannot be separated from the concurrent oil and geopolitical shock.

For USD, the release is supportive through the relative labor-resilience channel. Durability depends on payrolls, hiring flows, hours worked and participation rather than on one weekly claims observation.

The main alternative interpretation is that the labor market remains frozen rather than strong: companies are neither hiring aggressively nor dismissing workers. Under that configuration, unemployment can remain low because labor supply is restrained even while employment opportunities for entrants and displaced workers remain weak.

The decisive falsification test is a sustained joint rise in initial claims, continuing claims and both four-week averages, accompanied by deterioration in WARN notices, announced layoffs or payroll breadth.

FRIDAY 24 JUL 2026

UNITED STATES — S&P Global Flash Manufacturing / Services / Composite PMI (Jul)

Release Date: 24 Jul 2026 | Local Time: 15:45
Importance: ****

1. Reuters Data

S&P Global Mfg PMI Flash: 53,8 | Prior: 53,9 | Reuters Poll: 54,3 | Surprise: -0,50

S&P Global Svcs PMI Flash: 53,6 | Prior: 51,2 | Reuters Poll: 51,5 | Surprise: 2,10

S&P Global Comp PMI Flash: 53,6 | Prior: 51,9

2. Professional Market Commentary

The professional tape treated the publication as a services-led acceleration in activity, but not as an unqualified broad-demand reacceleration.

The Composite Output Index rose to an eight-month high, driven by the sharp services upside surprise. S&P Global and Reuters linked part of the services improvement to stronger consumer activity around the FIFA World Cup, Independence Day and other summer events, raising questions over the persistence of the July step-up.

Manufacturing remained expansionary but lost momentum. The headline index edged lower and the manufacturing output measure fell to a four-month low, consistent with some fading of the precautionary ordering and inventory-building impulse that had supported earlier factory activity.

The more concerning element was the price and supply-chain detail. Input costs accelerated amid higher energy, freight and tariff-related costs, selling-price inflation rose sharply, and supplier delays intensified as renewed Middle East disruption affected shipping routes.

Employment nevertheless returned to marginal growth after two months of decline.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

The primary signal is a meaningful reversal of the June services slowdown.

Signal hierarchy:

* services delivered the dominant upside surprise
* composite activity reached its strongest level since November 2025
* manufacturing conditions remained expansionary
* manufacturing output momentum weakened materially
* private-sector employment returned to marginal growth
* event-related consumer demand contributed to the services acceleration
* input-cost and selling-price inflation reaccelerated
* supply delays became more severe
* the growth improvement therefore arrived with a less favorable inflation mix

The activity signal is stronger than in June, but its quality is uneven. Services growth broadened enough to lift the composite decisively, while manufacturing output weakened despite the still-firm headline manufacturing PMI.

The distinction between current activity and persistence is important. World Cup and national-event spending represent real output, but they do not necessarily establish a durable household-demand run-rate. The July services jump therefore requires confirmation from final PMIs, consumer spending and August survey data.

By contrast, the price and delivery-time details may be more regime-relevant. Energy, freight, tariffs and supply disruption are simultaneously raising business costs and restoring firms’ willingness or ability to pass those costs into selling prices.

That produces a stagflationary survey configuration: faster near-term output, weaker manufacturing momentum and stronger price pressure.

State transition: reversal.

Context from prior regional live file:

May services had been close to stall speed, while June produced only modest stabilization. Manufacturing expansion had also become increasingly dependent on precautionary ordering, stock-building and supply-chain protection rather than clean final-demand acceleration. July reverses the services slowdown, but manufacturing softness and temporary demand support leave the durability of the broader growth reacceleration unconfirmed.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

The release tightens the near-term Federal Reserve constraint but does not create a deterministic policy trigger.

The combination of stronger services activity, marginally improving employment and faster selling-price inflation reduces the room for an easing interpretation. Ahead of the July FOMC meeting, the survey reinforces the argument that demand has not weakened enough to neutralize renewed supply-side inflation pressure.

The reaction-function implication remains conditional:

* confirmation from final PMIs, GDP and consumer spending would strengthen the growth-resilience branch
* persistence in selling-price inflation would reinforce the hawkish front-end risk
* fading event demand or normalization of energy and transport costs would weaken the signal
* further manufacturing-output deterioration would expose the composite rebound as increasingly services-dependent

For rates, the release creates a hawkish asymmetry at the front end rather than a clean long-end signal. Strong activity and prices can support higher policy-rate expectations, while supply-driven inflation and weaker manufacturing quality remain adverse for real growth.

For USD, the print is conditionally supportive through relative activity and policy restraint. A durable move requires confirmation from the FOMC, Q2 GDP and PCE rather than reliance on one event-boosted survey.

The decisive verification test is whether July’s growth-price combination survives after the temporary summer demand impulse fades.

UNITED STATES — New Home Sales (Jun)

Release Date: 24 Jul 2026 | Local Time: 16:00
Importance: ***

1. Reuters Data

New Home Sales-Units: 0,628M | Prior: 0,580M | Revised: 0,618M | Reuters Poll: 0,610M | Surprise: 0,0180M

2. Professional Market Commentary

The professional tape framed the report as a modest stabilization in new-home transactions rather than a housing recovery.

Sales rose to a 628,000 annualized pace, exceeding consensus, while May was revised substantially higher to 618,000 from the initially reported 580,000. The improvement ended two consecutive monthly declines, but sales remained below their June 2025 level.

Affordability remained the central constraint. The median sales price fell to $398,300, while inventory remained elevated at 485,000 units, equivalent to 9.3 months of supply at the current sales rate.

The volume improvement was concentrated geographically. Sales increased strongly in the South, while the West recorded a sharp decline, limiting the breadth of the national rebound.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

The report improves the recent volume trajectory, but the underlying housing configuration remains constrained.

Signal hierarchy:

* sales exceeded consensus
* May was revised from 580,000 to 618,000
* June sales rose modestly from the revised May base
* sales remained below their year-earlier level
* months’ supply stayed high at 9.3
* the median and average sales prices declined
* the share of transactions shifted toward lower-priced homes
* regional gains were dominated by the South
* sales in the West fell sharply
* financing and affordability constraints continued to shape both volumes and product mix

The upward revision is more important than the reported monthly increase. It removes much of the apparent May collapse and changes the sequence from uninterrupted deterioration to a more stable 618,000–628,000 run-rate.

However, the monthly gain is statistically weak. Census reported a wide confidence interval around the increase, meaning the agency could not establish that sales genuinely rose rather than remained broadly unchanged. Preliminary new-home-sales estimates also remain revision-sensitive.

The price detail is not a clean like-for-like house-price measure. Median-price movements reflect shifts in the regional, size and quality distribution of homes sold as well as changes in underlying prices. The higher share of lower-priced transactions and weaker sales in the more expensive West indicate that composition contributed materially to the decline.

The inventory position remains the main constraint. A 9.3-month supply ratio is inconsistent with a tight new-home market and indicates that builders still need price, size or financing adjustments to clear available stock.

State transition: stabilization.

Context from prior regional live file:

The prior USD housing sequence had deteriorated through weaker new-home sales, elevated supply and binding mortgage-rate constraints. June’s 628,000 pace and the upward May revision interrupt the volume decline, but elevated inventory and the shift toward lower-priced transactions keep the sector rate-capped. Housing moves from deterioration to tentative stabilization, not recovery.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

The release marginally reduces the housing-downside tail but does not change the broader policy reaction function.

For the Fed, the report shows that demand has not collapsed and that builders can still generate transactions through price and product adjustment. However, high months’ supply, lower year-on-year sales and the affordability-driven shift toward cheaper homes preserve housing as a restrictive-policy transmission channel.

The signal is therefore two-sided:

* the sales beat and upward revision weaken an immediate housing-contraction call
* the price mix and supply ratio show that stabilization remains costly for builders
* higher mortgage rates would likely require further concessions to sustain volumes
* lower long-term rates could generate a larger response because underlying demand has not disappeared

For rates, this is not strong enough to override the claims and inflationary PMI releases. It slightly reduces the growth downside attached to housing but does not provide evidence of a self-sustaining residential cycle.

For USD, the release has limited standalone relevance. Its main value is as confirmation that the economy retains a housing activity floor despite restrictive financing conditions.

The next verification test is whether sales remain near or above the revised May–June level without another large downward revision or further deterioration in prices and incentives.

H. CURRENCY MARKET-CONSENSUS SCAN

### Bottom line

Pair convention: EUR/USD, where a lower pair is a stronger USD.

The public institutional baseline entering the 20–24 July window still favored a gradual medium-term dollar retreat rather than a sustained extension of the June rebound. The Reuters June 26–July 1 FX strategist poll had EUR/USD at 1.16 by end-Q3, 1.17 at year-end and 1.18 in twelve months. MUFG’s 1 July outlook likewise targeted EUR/USD 1.16 in Q3 and 1.18 in Q4, explicitly arguing that the pair should recover as Fed hike expectations receded. At the same time, the public distribution was already unusually divided: Bank of America expected additional dollar appreciation through Q3, while Citi saw a high-risk downside scenario toward EUR/USD 1.11 if inflation surprised higher and the Fed repriced more hawkishly.

During this window, the tactical stronger-dollar camp gained ground. EUR/USD traded around 1.1402 on 21 July as renewed U.S.-Iran escalation, higher oil prices and rising Fed-hike odds supported the dollar. By 23 July, Brent had moved above $100, initial claims had fallen to 187k and EUR/USD dropped to 1.1372 as markets priced a 35.8% probability of a July Fed hike and an 81.4% probability of a September move. On 24 July, most major currencies were broadly steady against USD, but the dollar index was on course for its largest weekly rise in roughly a month and markets still saw about a one-in-three chance of an immediate Fed hike.

The key distinction is forecast change versus price convergence. The standing medium-term public-bank forecast cluster did not visibly reset during 20–24 July; instead, spot moved further away from the 1.16 Q3 median as the oil, tariff and Fed-risk distribution shifted in favor of the dollar. The week therefore strengthened tactical USD conviction without establishing that the medium-term softer-USD consensus had formally capitulated.

**Public-bank / strategist Q3–3M range:** The visible public sample was too thin for a robust base-case numerical range. The anchored central public target was EUR/USD 1.16 by end-Q3; Citi separately identified 1.11 as a non-base-case downside scenario under stronger inflation / Fed repricing.

**Constructive USD cluster:** EUR/USD around 1.14 or lower tactically, with Bank of America retaining a stronger-USD Q3 bias and Citi’s 1.11 level representing the hawkish-inflation tail.

**More cautious / tactical view:** EUR/USD around 1.16 by end-Q3, 1.17 at year-end and 1.18 on the later horizon as Fed hike expectations eventually recede.

**Bias at window close:** Tactical USD bullish / medium-term still softer USD. Spot was below the public Q3 central target and moving away from it as oil, tariffs and tightening expectations rebuilt the dollar’s rate and safe-haven support.

### What changed through the data window

The week opened with the dollar extending a multi-day rebound as renewed U.S.-Iran strikes and threats to Red Sea / Hormuz shipping pushed oil higher. On 21 July the dollar index reached 101.16 and EUR/USD fell to 1.1402, while the implied probability of a July Fed hike had recovered to 21.9% from roughly 11% the prior week and September-hike odds stood at 68.2%.

The move intensified on 23 July. Brent crossed $100, the U.S. labor market delivered an exceptionally low 187k initial-claims print, and EUR/USD fell to 1.1372. Markets raised the probability of a July hike to 35.8% and September to 81.4%. The contemporaneous FX logic was explicitly relative: the U.S. economy was viewed as more insulated than Europe or Japan from the energy shock, while higher oil simultaneously increased U.S. inflation and Fed-tightening risk.

On 24 July oil eased below $100, but the policy repricing did not fully reverse. New U.S. tariff announcements added another inflation channel, Treasury yields remained elevated and markets continued to see roughly a one-in-three chance of a Fed hike the following week. The dollar was broadly steady on the day but headed for its strongest weekly gain in about a month.

### Main consensus drivers

**Fed / rate differentials:**
The dominant change was the restoration of hike optionality. Softer June inflation had previously reduced the immediate tightening case, but oil, low claims and resilient activity rebuilt July and especially September hike expectations.

**Energy / geopolitical asymmetry:**
Higher oil supported USD through both safe-haven demand and relative macro insulation. Europe and Japan were viewed as more vulnerable to imported-energy deterioration, while the U.S. retained a stronger domestic-energy buffer.

**Tariffs / inflation risk:**
Fresh tariff action increased the probability that inflation pressure would persist even if oil later normalized. That strengthened the case for a longer-lived Fed premium rather than a purely war-driven dollar spike.

**Relative growth / labor resilience:**
Services acceleration and exceptionally low layoffs reduced the probability that the Fed would need to offset the cost shock with growth or employment support.

### Where consensus could be wrong

**Consensus too bullish USD:**
If oil retraced quickly, tariff pass-through proved weak and subsequent core inflation remained benign, the rebuilt hike premium could unwind and EUR/USD could move back toward the 1.16 Q3 public central target.

**Consensus too cautious USD:**
If oil / freight disruption persisted, tariffs broadened and resilient services / labor retention allowed the Fed to tighten without a material growth break, EUR/USD could stay below 1.14 and the 1.11 hawkish-tail scenario would become materially more relevant.

**Key falsification:**
Whether the oil-and-tariff shock produces persistent core inflation strong enough to validate a September Fed hike before U.S. growth and labor breadth deteriorate.

Sources used for this historical scan: Reuters FX strategist poll, 1 Jul 2026; MUFG Monthly Foreign Exchange Outlook, 1 Jul 2026; Reuters FX market reports, 21 Jul and 23 Jul 2026; Reuters global-markets report, 24 Jul 2026.

A. USD WEEK — MACRO SYNTHESIS

US growth remained resilient but increasingly bifurcated. Retail control, low claims and sharp regional manufacturing-survey gains preserved the domestic-demand and near-term activity floor, while flat manufacturing output and renewed deterioration across pending sales, builder confidence and single-family permits confirmed that hard industrial momentum remained narrow and restrictive financial conditions continued to transmit through housing. Labor stabilized in a low-firing configuration, but the week provided no evidence that weak national hiring flows had restarted.

Inflation improved materially at the consumer and producer levels, with softer shelter and benign core monthly readings providing genuine underlying relief, but the dominant headline contribution came from energy declines whose enabling conditions had already reversed. Accelerating nonfuel import prices, China-origin repricing and renewed Iran/Hormuz disruption prevented the CPI/PPI downside from becoming a broad disinflation regime. Fed communication fractured into three visible camps: Logan explicitly advocated a hike, Jefferson judged policy sufficiently restrictive, Waller remained hike-permissive but cautioned against overcorrection, and Warsh preserved the tightening option without guiding the next move. The July hike tail was materially reduced, but the September tightening branch remained live under an unusually high-uncertainty, no-forward-guidance regime.

Pending sales fell 5.4%, builder confidence stayed deeply contractionary at 34, buyer traffic weakened, concessions increased and single-family permits declined. Multifamily volatility lifted headline starts, but did not alter the rate-capped ownership and construction pipeline. Financial conditions continued to constrain rate-sensitive demand despite resilient consumption elsewhere.

Policy Constraint: ~
Supporting evidence:
The CPI/PPI downside surprises made a July hike difficult to justify and Jefferson judged the existing stance sufficiently restrictive, while Waller warned against overcorrecting. However, Logan explicitly called for a modest hike, Schmid retained a broad inflation-persistence concern, Warsh declined to signal the next move and renewed Iran/Hormuz pressure threatened to reverse the energy relief. The committee entered blackout three-way split: July hold remained the base case, but hawkish framing and a live September tightening option prevented a durable easing interpretation.

2. Professional Market Commentary

The professional tape treated the report as a substantial downside surprise with two distinct elements: a mechanically dominant energy reversal and a smaller but genuine improvement in underlying inflation.

Headline CPI declined 0.4% m/m as energy fell 5.7% and gasoline fell 9.7%. Core CPI was unchanged, bringing the annual core rate down to 2.6%. Shelter rose only 0.1%, while lower motor-vehicle insurance, communication, apparel, medical-care and used-vehicle prices contributed to the soft core result.

The dominant caveat was that the headline energy relief was already backward-looking. Renewed Gulf hostilities had pushed oil prices higher again before publication, increasing the probability that part of June’s headline decline would reverse.

Markets removed almost all probability of a July Fed hike and Treasury yields declined sharply. Later-year tightening remained live because underlying inflation was still above target and the energy reversal did not constitute a durable supply-shock resolution.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

This is a two-bucket report, with materially different signal quality across the two buckets.

Oil-reversible bucket:

energy fell 5.7% m/m

gasoline fell 9.7% m/m

the energy decline was sufficiently large to explain more than the entire headline CPI contraction

the monthly headline surprise was therefore dominated by a volatile component whose forward direction had already changed

the June print records temporary ceasefire and transit normalization rather than the renewed disruption prevailing at the time of release

The headline decline is mechanically real but weak as a forward inflation indicator.

Sticky-core bucket:

core CPI was unchanged m/m

shelter rose only 0.1%, its smallest monthly increase since January 2021

core goods declined 0.1% and were up only 0.8% y/y

apparel fell 0.6%

medical-care services fell 0.1%

airline fares remained elevated on an annual basis but were not a monthly disinflation contributor

food increased 0.2% and remained an unhelpful household-price component

Shelter is the highest-quality signal. It carries greater persistence than the energy reversal and is large enough in the CPI basket to matter materially if repeated.

Measurement hierarchy:

headline CPI materially overstates durable progress because of energy

core CPI shows genuine sequential improvement

shelter provides the most credible persistent disinflation signal

the CPI-to-core-PCE mapping remains less benign because the Fed’s preferred measure applies different weights

CPI-W’s decline to 327,075 is the mechanical counterpart of the broader price-level decline and adds no independent regime information

The report therefore validates part of the upstream easing seen in June surveys, but not through a clean generalized disinflation process. The strongest persistent signal is slower shelter; the largest numerical contribution is energy and is already vulnerable to reversal.

State transition: false dawn in headline inflation; stabilization-to-improvement in the sticky-core bucket.

Context from prior regional live file: The prior USD sequence had shown ISM manufacturing and services price indices falling sharply but remaining elevated, alongside a Fed that retained an inflation-contingent tightening bias. The inflation trajectory improves while remaining exposed to the same supply-shock variable that produced the prior acceleration.

2. Professional Market Commentary

The professional tape treated the release as a large and broad housing-demand disappointment.

the annual comparison returned slightly negative

pending contracts lead completed existing-home sales, usually by one or two months

South: -4.1% m/m, -0.9% y/y

West: -4.7% m/m, -1.1% y/y

Pending contracts are not completed transactions. Financing problems, inspections, appraisals and other contingencies can cause fallout before closing. The index nevertheless provides a leading read on future existing-home sales.

The release invalidates the idea that May’s improvement represented the beginning of a durable housing turn. Mortgage rates and record prices remain sufficiently restrictive to produce renewed weakness before broader employment losses have emerged.

State transition: deterioration — tentative contract-signing stabilization reversed through a large, nationally broad decline.

Context from prior regional live file: The earlier pending-sales sequence had moved from a one-month false dawn to conditional stabilization after consecutive positive readings. June breaks that sequence and restores the rate-capped housing interpretation. The forward transaction pipeline is weakening again before the latest energy and financing pressure fully reaches completed sales.

Policy mapping:

UNITED STATES — Import Prices MM / YY (Jun) Release Date: 17 Jul 2026 | Local Time: 14:30 Importance: ***

1. Reuters Data

Import Prices MM: 0,3% | Prior: 1,9% | Revised: 1,7% | Poll: -0,7% | Surprise: 1,00% Import Prices YY: 7,1% | Prior: 6,7% | Revised: 6,6%

2. Professional Market Commentary

The tape treated the report as the week’s principal hawkish counterpoint to CPI and PPI.

Import prices rose 0.3% against consensus for a 0.7% decline—a full percentage-point surprise—taking the annual rate to 7.1%, its largest increase since August 2022.

Fuel import prices declined 0.4%, but nonfuel import prices increased 0.4% for a seventh consecutive month. Capital-goods prices rose, with strength in computers, peripherals, semiconductors and machinery.

China import prices rose 0.9%, their largest monthly increase since January 2008. Import air-freight prices rose another 1.9% after a 19.1% May increase.

Export prices fell 0.6%, their first monthly decline since May 2025, but remained 10.2% higher y/y.

3. Comment — Economist Layer

This is the most regime-relevant inflation datapoint of the week after CPI and PPI because it isolates the non-reversible bucket at the border.

Signal hierarchy:

fuel imports fell 0.4%

petroleum declined 0.7%

natural-gas import prices rose 9.2%

nonfuel import prices rose 0.4%

nonfuel prices increased 4.2% y/y, their fastest pace since June 2022

nonfuel industrial supplies rose 1.2%

capital goods rose 0.4%

China prices rose 0.9%

import air-freight prices rose 1.9% m/m and 33.8% y/y

The fuel/nonfuel split maps directly onto the two-bucket framework. Fuel captured the temporary ceasefire-window relief; nonfuel prices continued accelerating.

The consensus error is important. Forecasters extrapolated lower energy across the aggregate index, but underlying foreign-goods pricing remained firm.

The China result is structurally significant but requires another month of confirmation. Because import-price indexes exclude tariffs, the increase measures foreign invoice-price behavior rather than the direct mechanical addition of customs duties.

Capital-goods pressure links imported inflation to the AI and investment cycle. This is demand- and capacity-related rather than a simple petroleum shock.

The report materially weakens the “broad cooling” interpretation of CPI and PPI. Consumer and domestic producer prices fell in June, but nonfuel border prices accelerated.

State transition: deterioration in the imported-inflation pipeline; sticky imported-cost pressure broadening.

Context from prior regional live file: The prior period had upstream pressure easing from extreme levels, supporting tentative moderation. June import prices interrupt that sequence at the border: nonfuel inflation accelerated to its fastest annual pace in four years and China pricing broke higher. The cost pipeline into goods inflation is re-steepening precisely as consumer-level prints improve.

4. HF Take — Strategist Layer

This is the release hawkish committee members can use to challenge the CPI/PPI relief narrative.

Conditional structure:

sustained nonfuel gains near 0.4% m/m would eventually threaten core-goods disinflation

a second strong China reading would suggest that exporter absorption is weakening

rising freight and capital-goods costs create a broader pipeline than oil alone

the report argues against extending the post-CPI front-end rally too aggressively

the market’s limited immediate reaction creates asymmetry if July data confirm the signal

Rates:

supports preservation of a September hike option

weakens the case for a rapid easing cycle

requires confirmation because pass-through lags are variable

USD:

imported-cost acceleration alongside a hike-permissive Fed is supportive through the policy channel

it is adverse through the terms-of-trade and real-income channels

relative energy resilience still favors the dollar against more import-dependent currencies during geopolitical escalation

Verification tests:
